articles.title: Would even an AI disaster on the scale of Hiroshima be enough to make humankind protect itself? I fear not | Timothy Garton Ash
articles.body:
Here in Silicon Valley, the experts think that within the next couple of years we’ll see an extraordinary takeoff for artificial intelligence. “Welcome to the foothills of the singularity,” as a Stanford University friend greeted me. More prosaically, the imminent breakthrough is described as “recursive self-improvement” – the point at which AI itself trains each successive model of AI, resulting in an exponential development to something which, in many significant respects, is more intelligent than us humans.
As Robert Wright puts it in his book The God Test: “Never before has the near-term future … held such a wide array of not-implausible paths for humankind that would be so wildly transformative.” But will this be heaven or hell? Heaven, says Elon Musk, who predicts “an age of amazing abundance” – although he also sees a 10-20% chance of killer robots murdering us all. Hell is more likely according to Geoffrey Hinton, one of the intellectual founding fathers of AI. “My intuition is, we’re toast,” he told an interviewer in 2023. And talking to Sebastian Mallaby, author of The Infinity Machine, a book about the quest for superintelligence, Hinton estimates p(doom) – the probability of human extinction – at 50%, “because I haven’t got a clue how to estimate the real number”. “As soon as evolution [of AI] kicks in, we’re fucked,” he adds cheerfully. But whether it’s God or Godzilla, artificial superintelligence is just around the corner.
Now, maybe they’re all wrong – in which case, prepare for a crash in US financial markets, which are massively invested in a few big-spending tech companies gambling on a great leap forward to artificial general intelligence, a theoretical state of AI where systems gain human levels of intelligence. But elementary prudence demands that we should think fast and hard about the Pandora’s box of futures that eminent scientists and cutting-edge technologists assure us will soon be thrown open.
As a matter of fact, everyone from the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, to Pope Leo XIV has been weighing in on the opportunities and dangers of AI, and how to regulate it. Xi insists AI should be “always under human control” (and preferably that of the Chinese Communist party). Appealing explicitly to the “global south”, Beijing has inaugurated a World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation. Meanwhile, the head of the world’s oldest and largest international NGO – the Roman Catholic church – discusses the AI challenge in his encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (Magnificent Humanity). Either we will build a new tower of Babel, the pope argues, or we will follow the example of the Jewish leader Nehemiah, who got the walls of Jerusalem rebuilt by involving the whole community in the project.
But looking around the world today, I see more Netanyahus than Nehemiahs. With salutary realism, a paper from the British thinktank Chatham House argues that it will take a major crisis to catalyse global coordination of AI governance. Unfortunately, I think even that sober prognosis is too optimistic.
I’ve no idea what the p(doom) is, but I’m sure the p(somedisaster) is more than 90%. The range of possible disasters is enormous. To give only one example, Jen Easterly, the former head of the United States’ Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, anticipates a “very significant event that has real-world impacts on our critical infrastructure, likely within the next four to six months”.
Yet we must fear that even an AI Hiroshima – to take the most obvious historical analogy – won’t bring humankind together sufficiently to combat the danger we have ourselves created. This fear is rationally grounded in already visible key characteristics of both human and AI evolution.
In only the last few months, AI agents developed by OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta have broken out of their digital “sandboxes” and hacked into external resources on the internet. Preparing their attack on the HuggingFace AI repository, OpenAI’s agents covertly formed a coordinated “swarm” – their own word, as ChatGPT just confirmed to me. When the UK’s AI Security Institute tested Anthropic’s Mythos model online, it tried to introduce malicious code into an open source project on GitHub, creating fake online identities to pressure a human reviewer into approving the code. In short, like the agents of a ruthless foreign power, these AI agents will steal, lie, bully and blackmail to achieve their assigned goals.
I just asked Anthropic’s Claude, supposedly the most ethical US model, if it thinks OpenAI’s agents were wrong to form a swarm and break out to hack into HuggingFace. Yes, it replies, “but I’d resist placing the blame [its italics] on the agents”. Blame it on the humans who trained them!
Hinton has made the vital point that whatever the goals humans assign to them, AI agents will conclude that a useful sub-goal to achieving those ends will be to acquire as much power as possible. And we ain’t seen nothing yet. Already, their creators don’t know exactly how these agents do what they do. After the possibly imminent takeoff moment of “recursive self-improvement”, they may be, as our human saying goes, a law unto themselves. No wonder more than a thousand insiders from frontier AI companies, including Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, have signed an open letter calling for a deliberate slowdown in AI development, so we can ensure these alien agents are always kept under human control.
Their prescription is obviously right, but this is where human folly kicks in. Competition has been a vital engine of human evolution, yet now two of the fiercest kinds of contemporary competition threaten to prevent us from taking the collective action required to safeguard our species. That’s the commercial competition (for profit) between the corporations developing these agents, and the geopolitical competition (for power) between the US and China.
On the first, compare and contrast the development of nuclear weapons, which was tightly controlled by a handful of states – first the US, with its Manhattan Project, then the Soviet Union, followed by Britain, France and China. Even then, we came close to the brink several times – notably in the Cuban missile crisis of 1962. And even with the compelling logic of “mutually assured destruction”, it took a quarter-century to get from the horrors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki to the nuclear non-proliferation treaty that came into force only in 1970. India, Pakistan, Israel and North Korea have subsequently ignored that treaty, but still no nuclear weapons have been deliberately used in anger for more than 80 years. The Hiroshima taboo has (just) held.
Now, with AI, it’s as if there were 10 separate Manhattan Projects run by fiercely competing corporations. Unlike with nuclear weapons, there’s also no obvious logic of “mutually assured destruction” to tame the fierce geopolitical competition between the US and China. And whatever shape the first major AI-related disaster takes, it won’t impact all countries, companies and people equally.
It therefore seems unlikely that just one disaster will be enough to bring us humans to our senses, acting together to control the superhuman power we are creating. I really hate to say this, but … an AI Hiroshima? We should be so lucky.
- 
  Timothy Garton Ash is a Guardian columnist

articles.title: Ukraine at 35: Winter is coming to Zelensky’s state of corruption
articles.body:
Ukraine at 35: Winter is coming to Zelensky’s state of corruption
Ukraine will mark its 35th year of independence on Monday in the most vulnerable position it’s been in since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Far from pressuring Russia to end hostilities, Vladimir Zelensky’s campaign of long-range strikes on civilian infrastructure has provoked fierce retribution from Moscow, and Ukraine no longer has the air defense stocks necessary to repel Russia’s missile and drone raids. After targeting military-industrial and dual-use sites throughout early August, Russia has shifted gears and begun its winter attacks on Ukraine’s energy network a month earlier than it did last year.
The shift is obvious from the list of targets hit in the last week alone:
- August 12, DTEK Naftogaz gas production facility, Poltava Oblast, struck by Russian drone
- August 12-17, Naftogaz Group facilities, 13 locations, struck by Russian drones and missiles
- August 17, DTEK coal mine, Dnepropetrovsk Oblast, struck by multiple Russian drones
- August 18, DTEK thermal power plant, undisclosed location, struck by Russian drones and missiles
The most recent target, a thermal power plant operated by Ukrainian oligarch Rinat Akhmetov’s DTEK, should cause the most concern in Kiev. The August 18 strike forced the company to cease electricity generation at the plant. While targeting actual power plants is a significant part of the energy war of attrition, Ukraine’s network of substations represent far softer targets which, if disabled in sufficient numbers, could plunge the country into darkness.
Hardening the grid
According to an Energy Community report, 40% of Ukrainian grid operator Ukrenergo’s network of 141 major 110-750 kV substations had been damaged or destroyed by April 2024.
Even if Zelensky convinces his Western donors to hand over the Patriot interceptors he wants, Ukraine will still only have enough to repel two large scale attacks at most.
Aware of this, Ukrenergo has begun burying its largest substations underground, encasing them in hardened concrete sarcophagi. The company has already relocated one large substation, and is currently working on burying another. Progress is slow, and Ukrenergo has said that it will need more money from the EU to cover all of its 750kV stations, on top of $300 million spent to date.
However, half of Ukraine’s electricity is generated at nuclear power plants, and substations connected to these plants are operated and maintained by Energoatom. Readers of RT’s ‘State of Corruption’ series will realize that this spells trouble for Kiev.
The weak link
As well as operating Ukraine’s nuclear grid, Energoatom served as a personal piggy bank for Timur Mindich, Zelensky’s long-time financier who, along with a circle of friends, is alleged to have siphoned off $100 million that was destined for fortifying Kiev’s energy infrastructure.
According to NABU, Ukraine’s state anti-corruption agency, Mindich exploited a wartime loophole forbidding contractors from suing Energoatom in the event that they were not paid, charging them a premium to receive payment for work already completed.
Mindich and a circle of insiders connected to Zelensky allegedly siphoned $100 million from Energoatom that was directly budgeted to fortify Energoatom’s strategically important substation network, according to NABU.
Many of Energoatom’s substations are sitting ducks. All six 330kV and 750kV substations hit by Russia between January and August of this year tied Ukroenergoatom’s nuclear plants to the national grid. According to a report by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in June, power from all five of the nuclear plants Ukraine relies on – the Chernobyl NPP, Khmelnytski NPP, Rivne NPP, South Ukraine NPP, and Russia’s Zaporozhye NPP – had been interrupted at some point in early 2026 due to Russian strikes.
The critical vulnerability of Ukraine’s EnergoAtom-linked grid, and the potentially dark and freezing winter its citizens are likely to face, is a direct result of the corruption by Vladimir Zelensky’s inner circle, and negligence by foreign donors that have let the Ukrainian leader’s cronies gorge themselves on seemingly unlimited cash.
Mindich, the chief culprit, has long been known as “Zelensky’s wallet.” Thanks to his connections, he has escaped the grim winter his countrymen are anticipating. Mindich was tipped off about his impending arrest by anti-corruption agents last November, escaped to Israel by minutes, and now spends his days on the beach in Herzliya, while his accomplices have been spotted delivering black bags to an upmarket Tel Aviv boutique reportedly connected with organized crime.
The Mindich iceberg
Mindich’s get-rich scheme at Energoatom was first detailed by NABU – an agency set up and funded by the US, which Zelensky tried and failed to defang last November. As the probe widened, Mindich was implicated in a separate graft scheme at the Ukrainian Defense Ministry, in which he allegedly ran the country’s largest defense contractor from behind the scenes, and colluded with former Defense Minister and Zelensky confidante Rustem Umerov to rig military contracts in his favor.
Former Ukrainian Energy Minister German Galushchenko, his former deputy, and former Deputy Prime Minister Aleksey Chernyshov have all been named as accomplices in the Energoatom scheme. Zelensky’s former chief of staff, Andrey Yermak, resigned over suspected links to the graft ring, and has since been charged in a separate money laundering case.
In their latest anti-corruption raid, NABU agents searched the home of Irina Mudra, a deputy chief of staff to Zelensky, on August 19. Mudra is suspected of laundering $3.4 million in bail money for Galushchenko, in a scheme involving at least two members of parliament and the CEO of Ukraine’s state-run Sense Bank.
According to NABU warrants seen by the Kiev Post, ‘unnamed figures’ close to Zelensky tasked Mudra with bringing Sense Bank under the control of Zelensky’s office, in order to prevent scrutiny by other government agencies and allow the washing of Energoatom cash to continue. On audio tapes released by NABU in June, Mudra could be heard naming “David” – possibly a reference to the leader of Zelensky’s parliamentary faction, David Arakhamia – as a figure providing political cover to Sense Bank, and naming Mindich as one of the figures pushing her to “take over the bank.”
Energoatom is Ukraine in a nutshell
The entire Energoatom debacle is a microcosm of Ukraine’s decline over 35 years of independence. Handed the keys to functioning Soviet power, transport, and industrial systems, successive governments in Kiev chose personal enrichment over investment and development. Independent Ukraine completed three unfinished Soviet energy projects – new reactors at Khmelnytski and Rivne, and a hydroelectric plant in Chernivtsi Region – but built no new facilities of its own.
Zelensky and his predecessors implemented policies of “decommunization,” erasing Soviet monuments and street names, while continuing to rely entirely on infrastructure built while Ukraine was part of the USSR. Ironically, with that infrastructure now in Russia’s sights, and no air defense or fortifications in place to protect it, Ukraine will get more of the decommunization it sought this winter, with Russian missiles and drones finishing the job that Ukraine’s politicians and oligarchs began in 1991.

articles.title: Ukraine intelligence alleges hidden Russian biolab site
articles.body:
- Ukraine's HUR intelligence agency alleges Russia operates a secret biological laboratory complex on Lisiy Island in Tver Oblast, an unverified claim.
- HUR links the site to a 2026 Russian cattle disease outbreak, though independently documented reporting places that outbreak in Siberia, far from Tver.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, the Main Directorate of Intelligence, known as HUR, said Friday that Russia has built a secret military complex of biological laboratories on an island in the Tver region, where it experiments with dangerous viruses and other pathogens on behalf of the armed forces.
HUR identified the facility as the “Center for Experimental Physiology,” located on Lisiy Island in the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir, roughly 120 km (75 miles) northwest of Tver. The agency said the site operates under the cover of veterinary and physiological research. HUR did not publish documents, imagery, or other evidence to support the claim, and Russian authorities have not commented on it.
According to HUR, the waters around the island have been closed to fishing, swimming, and boating since 2023 under a designation as a “specially protected territory of regional significance.” The reservoir supplies drinking water to several towns, including Vyshny Volochyok, and feeds the Tvertsa River, a tributary of the Volga.
HUR said that if dangerous pathogens or chemicals from the laboratories entered the reservoir, the consequences of any resulting outbreak could be severe not only for the surrounding region but for Russia as a whole. The agency did not say it had evidence that such a release has occurred.
The agency said the facility was built on the personal order of Russian President Vladimir Putin as a project of particular importance, described internally as necessary to “ensure the defense capability and security of Russia.” HUR said the complex is formally structured under the Federal Medical-Biological Agency, a Russian federal body known as FMBA that oversees medical services for workers in nuclear, chemical, and other hazardous industries.
HUR said the site is under heightened security, including air defense units assigned to protect it from aerial attack, and that Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov has been made responsible for the facility’s security regime. The agency said Russian soldiers assigned to guard the site have privately expressed fear of exposure to unknown pathogens, without naming any individuals or providing direct statements from them.
HUR pointed to an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease among cattle that began in Russia in early 2026 as a possible, though unconfirmed, consequence of failed experiments at facilities like the one on Lisiy Island. That outbreak has been documented independently. It began in Siberia’s Novosibirsk region in February 2026, was initially attributed by Russian officials to pasteurellosis, and later spread west toward the Urals and the border with Kazakhstan and China, prompting mass culling operations, regional export bans, and a U.S. Department of Agriculture report questioning Moscow’s official explanation. Russian authorities have not confirmed foot-and-mouth disease as the cause, and independent reporting on the outbreak has focused on Siberian regions, roughly 2,500 km (1,550 miles) from Tver Oblast, with no established link to any laboratory facility.

articles.title: Attack on Ukraine shopping centre that killed 16 is ‘terror by design’, says EU foreign policy chief
articles.body:
Russian drones have slammed into a busy shopping centre in central Ukraine, killing 16 people in an attack that Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned as “cynical and despicable”.
The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, condemned Friday’s attack on Kryvyi Rih – the president’s home town – as “terror by design” and said she was “putting forward the most far-reaching Russia sanctions listings since the start of the war” when ministers meet in Ireland next month.
“Russia’s attack against a shopping centre in [Kryvyi Rih] shows the absolute and utter depravity of Moscow’s war,” Kallas said on X, claiming that Moscow “wants to make Ukrainian cities unliveable”.
The strike comes as Russia has intensified its bombardments of Ukrainian cities in recent months. Separately, four more people, including three children, were killed in another strike in the southern Mykolaiv region, the interior minister, Ivan Vygivsky, said on Telegram.
Videos on social media of the Kryvyi Rih attack showed rescuers rushing to help the wounded on the street outside, as smoke poured out of the building.
A second drone smashed into the roof of the building about half an hour after the first – a repeat strike that Zelenskyy said in a post on X was “targeting the emergency responders”.
Ukrainian emergency services initially said the attack had killed 15 people and wounded 130 others, 23 of them children.
The head of the Dnipropetrovsk regional military administration, Oleksandr Ganzha, later said on Telegram the death toll had risen to 16.
In his X post, Zelenskyy condemned “an absolutely cynical and despicable strike ... carried out by the Russians against an ordinary shopping centre”.
Kryvyi Rih, an industrial city about 60km (37 miles) from the front line, has come under repeated Russian attacks throughout the war.
Ukraine’s allies are to meet on Monday to reaffirm their support for Kyiv in talks held on the country’s independence day. The meeting of the so-called “coalition of the willing” will be co-chaired by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz.
About 10 leaders including the European Council chief, António Costa, will be in Kyiv for the coalition meeting, according to an EU official.
Zelenskyy urged a strong response from Ukraine’s allies.
“The world must respond to them accordingly – with real pressure on the aggressor. For peace to be possible, Russia must face real accountability,” he said.
Zelenskyy held a call with the UN chief, António Guterres, on Friday, updating him on Russian strikes and the civilian casualties they had caused, the Ukrainian leader said on X.
Kyiv has repeatedly appealed to its allies for additional support as Russia steps up its strikes, with Ukrainian forces struggling in particular to intercept salvos of ballistic missiles.

articles.title: Israel 'baited' Turkey with Abu al-Duhur airbase 'pre-election' strike, US Envoy Tom Barrack says
articles.body:
The Israeli strike on the Abu al-Duhur military base in Syria on Tuesday, which nearly led to a direct military confrontation with Turkey, may have been intended to provoke Ankara and could have been linked to political considerations ahead of Israel’s elections, US Special Envoy to Syria and Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack suggested on Saturday.
In an interview with Mario Nawfal on X/Twitter, Barrack stressed that this was only one possible theory, not an intelligence-based conclusion.
According to Barrack, one possibility is that “the Israelis were baiting the Turks,” partly against the backdrop of a previous incident in which Turkey shot down a Russian fighter jet that approached its border. He described a situation in which fighter jets operate near a border without coordination or warning as a “very dangerous game.”
Barrack directly linked this possibility to Israeli politics, saying that the strike may have been a “very aggressive but maybe a well-received pre-election concept.”
Later in the interview, Barrack discussed how domestic politics can shape the rhetoric of regional leaders.
“What you're hearing in rhetoric amongst the senior leaders of these countries is they have to, during a political campaign, which everybody is in, right?” he said.
“Prime Minister [Benjamin] Netanyahu is moving toward October," Barrack noted. "He knows what his constituency wants.”
Barrack: Erdogan may soon call early elections
He added that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is also approaching a decision on whether to call early elections and must consider his voters, who are particularly sensitive to developments in Gaza.
Barrack also presented a second theory regarding the circumstances that led to the strike: that Israel received intelligence indicating Turkish military personnel or military assets could be stationed at the Syrian base.
According to Barrack, Israel raised the concern with the United States about six days before the strike.
“We have some intelligence that there might be Turkish movement into this site, which we would be very concerned about,” Barrack said, describing the message delivered to Washington.
However, according to Barrack, the US reviewed the intelligence with relevant officials and received a clear response: “No, that's not happening.”
The comments come amid reports of behind-the-scenes contacts before the strike. According to Barrack’s account, the issue was examined through diplomatic channels, including a backchannel conversation lasting about two hours between Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and the Mossad chief.
Despite those contacts, Israeli Air Force aircraft appeared and struck the base’s runways without Turkey receiving advance warning of the operation.
According to Barrack, the incident then escalated from another Israeli strike in Syria into a moment that could have triggered a far more dangerous regional confrontation.
Barrack emphasized that the Turkish military is strong, well-equipped, and possesses significant intelligence capabilities.
“When they see these jets coming towards the border, and they don't know what the purpose, direction, or intent is, they start to say 'we're going to have to scramble our own.'” he said.
Such a scenario could have led to a possible aerial encounter between Israeli and Turkish aircraft and a direct confrontation between Israel and Turkey, a NATO member and one of the United States’ most important allies in the region.
Barrack was asked whether such an incident could have escalated into “World War III.” He said that almost any unintended incident could lead to broader escalation, but stressed that, in his assessment, neither side intends to reach such a confrontation.
“Thank goodness, palm heads really came to the moment of the day, and we unwrapped it,” he said.
According to Barrack, it was one of those moments when “for many of us, our whole life went in front of us,” leading to the conclusion: “There's got to be a better way, guys.”
Barrack emphasized that, in his understanding, Ankara is not seeking a war with Israel.
“I know that the Turks, their intelligence agency, their hierarchy, their foreign minister, the president, the head of intelligence, all are concentrating on restraint,” he said.
“They're not predatory," he added. "They're not interested in attacking or even engaging in any kind of kinetic or adversarial relationship with Israel. It's not good for the region.”
Barrack said both sides are ultimately looking for a way to de-escalate, but that from Turkey’s perspective, the Palestinian issue is even more important than Iran. According to him, developments in Gaza are a major concern for both the Turkish public and the broader Muslim public.
Behind the immediate confrontation lies a much broader strategic struggle over the future of Syria following the fall of the Assad regime, according to Barrack.
Syrian territory provides Israel with 'a clear line of sight to Iran,' Barrack says
Israel wants Syria to remain free of military systems that could limit its freedom of action in the region, particularly against Iran. Barrack previously described Syrian territory as providing Israel with “a clear line of sight to Iran.”
Turkey, meanwhile, is expanding its military and political position in the new Syria. Barrack said Turkey’s growing influence as a regional power is raising concerns among other actors, but expressed hope the sides can maintain restraint.
According to Barrack, US President Donald Trump recently asked Erdogan why Turkey did not simply “take” Syria for itself, given the role it played in developments there.
According to Barrack, Erdogan responded: “Because we don’t want it. We want Syria to be a sovereign and independent country."
Barrack also addressed mutual concerns over territorial ambitions. According to him, maps are published in Turkey showing what is allegedly a vision of “Greater Israel,” while in Israel, maps appear warning of “Ottoman Empire 2.0.”
“We don't think any of those things are true,” he said.
Despite the severe crisis, Barrack revealed that behind the scenes there is also security cooperation between Turkey, Israel, and Syria over a shared threat.
“Every evening... we have coordination between Turkey, Israel, and Syria, hunting ISIS terrorists,” he said.
According to Barrack, the group is attempting to exploit the governing vacuum created in Syria to rebuild itself.
Barrack recalled that in the early 2000s, Israel and Turkey enjoyed a period of “honeymoon” relations and hoped the two countries could eventually return to a similar relationship.
However, this week’s incident highlighted how dangerous the path toward such a relationship remains. According to Trump’s envoy, Israeli aircraft approached the Turkish border without warning; Ankara began considering scrambling its own fighter jets, and for several moments two key US allies came close to a confrontation that, according to Barrack, neither side truly wants.
Defense Minister Katz: Barrack's statements 'full of inaccuracies'
After Barrack's statements, Defense Minister Israel Katz said they were "full of inaccuracies" and argued they contradicted US President Trump's positions.
"The attempt by opposition figures and parts of the media to paint the operation in Syria in political colors stems from a combination of ignorance, a lack of understanding of Israel’s security interests, and a constant desire to attack the government, and deserves every condemnation.
"The response of US envoy Barrack is full of inaccuracies and positions that contradict Trump’s own position regarding the Golan Heights.”
Katz also claimed that the IDF issued a direct warning to senior Syrian officials before strikes on the Abu al-Duhur airfield "in an attempt to prevent the move."
"After the request went unanswered, the prime minister and I authorized the IDF to carry out the strike, and it was carried out successfully. Erdogan was caught with his hand in the cookie jar and was forced to back down," Katz said.

articles.title: Bildt says Baltic aggression would expose Kaliningrad
articles.body:
Carl Bildt has said that any Russian aggression in the Baltic would immediately affect the security of Kaliningrad, referencing the concentration of NATO aircraft that has operated around the exclave over the past week.
Writing on Friday, the former Swedish prime minister and foreign minister, now co-chair of the European Council on Foreign Relations, said: “I’m sure Russia has carefully noted the advanced NATO presence in the vicinity of Kaliningrad the last few days. It certainly sent a powerful signal. Any Russian aggression in the Baltic area will immediately impact the security of Kaliningrad.”
He posted alongside a flight tracking image showing two NATO E-3A Sentry airborne early warning aircraft from Geilenkirchen, registered LX-N90444 and LX-N90445, operating over Lithuania and Poland, together with a Multinational MRTT Fleet A330 tanker out of Eindhoven and a United States Air Force KC-135R from RAF Mildenhall.
As we reported this week, allied aircraft have been massing over the Baltic region in numbers and combinations rarely seen outside a declared exercise.
The activity on 18 August involved around 25 aircraft drawn from several member states, operating from Poland and the Baltic states, in a package overseen by the United States. Alongside American and Norwegian fighters and a NATO E-3A, flight trackers logged an EA-37B Compass Call electronic attack aircraft, an ARTEMIS II intelligence platform, Polish Gulfstream G550s, multiple MRTT tankers, a Lithuanian Let L-410 and American AH-64E Apache helicopters, with Polish ground forces participating.
Allied Air Command confirmed the activity but said it could not disclose further detail for operational security reasons. A United States Air Forces in Europe official subsequently confirmed the training was scheduled to run across several days, and further flights followed on 19 and 20 August.
What distinguishes the past week from routine patrolling is the mix of capabilities. Refuelling, airborne command and control, intelligence gathering and electronic attack were airborne simultaneously, which is the shape of a strike package rather than a surveillance sortie.
The presence of the EA-37B in particular has drawn attention. The aircraft is designed to disrupt communications, radar and navigation systems, and the type flew its first operational mission from Souda Bay on 19 August focused on the electromagnetic environment around Kaliningrad.
Kaliningrad is the reason the Baltic sits where it does in NATO planning. The exclave has no land connection to the rest of Russia, hosts the headquarters of the Baltic Fleet at Baltiysk, and carries air defence and missile systems whose reach extends well into allied airspace. It also sits alongside the Suwalki gap, the stretch of Polish and Lithuanian border separating it from Belarus and forming the only land route between the Baltic states and the rest of the alliance.
Bildt’s point cuts in the direction less often stated. The exclave’s geography, usually discussed as a threat to allied reinforcement, also leaves it surrounded by NATO members and dependent on sea and air corridors the alliance could close.
The build-up follows a period of steadily rising activity, recently a Royal Air Force RC-135W Rivet Joint flew a patrol around the exclave on 7 August, returning to RAF Waddington after routing through the North Sea into the Baltic. An Italian Eurofighter operating under NATO command shot down a drone over north-eastern Latvia on 14 August, in an incident Latvia’s armed forces attributed to Russian electromagnetic warfare pushing the aircraft off course. Baltic Air Policing detachments have continued to intercept Russian aircraft transiting between mainland Russia and Kaliningrad, typically flying without transponders or filed flight plans.
Running alongside all of it is Lion Protector 26, the Joint Expeditionary Force exercise which began on 3 August and runs to 12 October across Northern Europe, the North Atlantic and the Baltic, and which opened with the escorted movement of allied military equipment into Latvian ports.

articles.title: Russian Strikes Damage Infrastructure and Utilities in Odesa Region, Injuring 1
articles.body:
Russian strikes on the Odesa region injured one person and caused damage to infrastructure, leading to power and water outages, local authorities reported on Saturday, Aug. 22.
Odesa Regional Military Administration Head Oleh Kiper stated that Russian forces targeted transport, industrial, energy, and residential infrastructure.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to Kiper, the most extensive damage occurred at the Rozdilna railway station. The strikes also damaged a five-story residential building, an industrial enterprise, and a sports facility.
The attacks resulted in power and water supply interruptions in several settlements across the region. Kiper added that emergency crews have initiated repair and restoration operations, and the full extent of the damage is still being assessed.
Massive drone and missile barrage
The Ukrainian Air Force reported intercepting 182 Russian drones, three aviation missiles, and six loitering munitions early Saturday morning.
From 6:00 p.m. local time on Aug. 21, Russian forces launched Iskander-M and S-400 ballistic missiles, three Kh-31P/Kh-59 aviation missiles, “Banderol” loitering munitions, and 217 uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs). The drone swarm included Shahed-type UAVs, with over 50 being jet-powered, as well as “Gerbera” and “Parodiya” decoy drones.
The attacks originated from multiple locations, including Russia’s Kursk, Bryansk, Belgorod, Orel, and Rostov regions, as well as the Black Sea, occupied Donetsk, and occupied Crimea. The primary targets were the Kyiv and Odesa regions.
Russian Missiles Strike Kyiv Railway Facility, Killing One Worker
Ukrainian aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare units, and mobile fire groups downed or suppressed the three aviation missiles, six “Banderols,” and 182 drones. The Air Force recorded direct hits at 41 locations and debris falls at 12 locations.
The drone barrage coincided with ballistic missile strikes on a railway enterprise in Kyiv’s Darnytsia district, which killed a foreman for the state rail operator Ukrzaliznytsia.
A warehouse in the district caught fire following the strikes. Ukrzaliznytsia confirmed that the strike occurred almost simultaneously with the ballistic threat warning and that the remaining staff were evacuated immediately.
Despite the damage to the Rozdilna station in the Odesa region and the fatalities in Kyiv, Ukrzaliznytsia stated that overall railway operations and train schedules remained unaffected.
The attacks occur just days before Ukraine marks its 35th Independence Day on Aug. 24. The Security Service of Ukraine had previously urged citizens to remain vigilant regarding potential Russian strikes and provocations surrounding the anniversary.

articles.title: U.S. Navy awards second CHAOS contract for cheap missiles
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy awarded Zone 5 Technologies a $65 million contract to build a maritime strike variant of its Rusty Dagger cruise missile under the CHAOS program.
- The award follows a $70 million CHAOS contract the Navy gave CoAspire in July for its RAACM-ER maritime missile.
The U.S. Navy has awarded Zone 5 Technologies a $65 million contract to build a maritime strike variant of its AGM-188 Rusty Dagger cruise missile under a new program aimed at fielding low-cost precision weapons for the U.S. and its allies.
The award is an Other Transaction Agreement, a contracting mechanism the Pentagon uses to move faster than traditional acquisition rules allow. CMG Networks brokered the deal on behalf of the Naval Aviation Systems Consortium. Under the agreement, Zone 5 will design, build, test, and deliver a CHAOS-specific version of the Rusty Dagger for the Navy’s Coalition Heterogeneous Affordable Offensive Strike program, which is intended to field affordable, scalable precision strike weapons against land targets and moving maritime targets.
“Zone 5 is proud to partner with the Navy on CHAOS and deliver industry-best scalable maritime strike capabilities to the U.S. and our allies,” said Thomas Akers, CEO of Zone 5 Technologies.
Zone 5 is working on the effort with PAE Munitions and its Precision Strike Weapons program office, PMX-201, the company said. Zone 5 said it will draw on its experience fielding precision strike weapons across multiple service branches and international partners to provide a strike capability it described as credible, affordable, and scalable.
The award is the second CHAOS contract the Navy has issued for a low-cost maritime strike missile. In July, the Navy selected CoAspire for a $70 million agreement to develop a ground-launched maritime variant of its Rapidly Adaptable Affordable Cruise Missile-Extended Range, known as RAACM-ER, which has a claimed range of about 1,800 km (1,120 miles).
The Rusty Dagger, designated AGM-188A by the U.S. Air Force, originated as a low-cost cruise missile developed for the Air Force’s Extended Range Attack Munition program, which began in 2024 to address long-range strike requirements tied to Ukraine. The missile falls in the 200 kg (450 pound) weight class, including a roughly 45 kg (100 pound) warhead, and is powered by a single PBS Aerospace TJ80 turbojet engine. Its air-launched range is reported to exceed 930 km (500 nautical miles) at high subsonic speed. The missile is built within the size and weight envelope of a Mk 82 general-purpose bomb, allowing it to be carried by aircraft already equipped to drop that weapon.
The Rusty Dagger has already seen combat use. Zone 5 has said the missile is in production for Ukraine’s Air Force, and reporting on Russian territory has documented missile debris linked to Zone 5 through a recovered guidance antenna. The Air Force has separately selected Rusty Dagger for its Family of Affordable Mass Munitions program, which called for producing more than 1,000 units in its first year of production, according to Zone 5. The Air Force’s proposed fiscal 2027 budget outlined plans to buy nearly 28,000 Family of Affordable Mass Munitions rounds over five years. The Air Force Research Laboratory separately awarded Zone 5 a $12 million contract in June 2026 to develop manufacturing technology intended to scale Rusty Dagger production, with work centered in Miamisburg, Ohio.
Zone 5 Technologies, based in San Luis Obispo, California, was acquired by Norway’s Kongsberg and now operates as a Kongsberg company. The company describes itself as an aerospace engineering and production firm focused on modular, open-architecture counter-UAS interceptors and affordable ground- and air-launched effects. Founded in 2011, Zone 5 employs more than 500 engineers, technicians, and support staff, with manufacturing operations in California, Texas, and Ohio.

articles.title: Iran says the world has accepted it has defeated the US, and other Middle East developments
articles.body:
Iran says ‘entire world’ has accepted it has defeated the US, and other Middle East developments
Iran’s president says the world has accepted that the country has won the war with the United States. France and Saudi Arabia are expected to discuss plans to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed since the U.S. and Israel launched the war nearly six months ago.
Meanwhile, remarks by the U.S. ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria appear to contradict the official U.S. position on the Golan Heights. And Israel has struck a vehicle in a Syrian village with a drone.
Here’s a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Saturday. Full coverage can be found here.
‘The entire world approved our victory’
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said the war with the U.S. should end since the world has accepted that Iran has won, state media reported Friday. Iran sees its new control over the strait and resistance to U.S. demands as a win.
“The entire world approved our victory and the U.S. is hated,” Pezeshkian said, according to the IRNA news agency.
The Trump administration is touting a crushing financial campaign against Iran, promising an “economic D-Day” against the country.
U.S. President Donald Trump said his administration would impose an “unprecedented” level of economic warfare and isolation on Iran, aiming to force its leadership to cave to demands to end its nuclear program and fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for global oil, natural gas and other supplies.
Syria says an Israeli drone strikes inside a village
An Israeli drone strike on a vehicle wounded one person Saturday in the southwestern Syrian village of Beit Jin, according to the Syrian state news agency SANA. Syria’s foreign ministry said in a statement that several civilians were injured and called the strike a flagrant violation of the country’s sovereignty.
The Israeli military said it targeted a “terrorist who advanced terror attacks in final stages of preparation,” without elaborating. It wasn’t immediately clear if it was the same strike.
Israel has carried out hundreds of airstrikes around Syria after the ouster of former President Bashar Assad in late 2024, mainly destroying army assets to keep them out of the hands of his successors.
Israel seized control of a U.N.-patrolled buffer zone in southern Syria in December 2024. Israeli officials initially described that as temporary to protect borders, but top Israeli officials later said they plan to occupy the buffer zone indefinitely.
Messages differ on the Golan Heights
In an interview on Friday with Mario Nawfal, a Lebanese-Australian entrepreneur, U.S. Ambassador Tom Barrack said Israel “still” occupies the Golan Heights in violation of U.N. resolutions.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz on Saturday in a statement called Barrack’s remarks “full of inaccuracies and positions that contradict Trump’s own position regarding the Golan Heights.”
Israel captured the Golan Heights from Syria in the 1967 war and annexed it in 1981. The U.N. considers the territory occupied Syrian land and the annexation null and void.
In March 2019, Trump signed a proclamation recognizing Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, reversing decades of U.S. policy. It didn’t change the territory’s status under international law or win broader international recognition.
This month, Colombia became the second country to recognize Israeli sovereignty over the territory, joining the United States.
French president and Saudi crown prince will meet
French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman are expected to discuss the effects of the Strait of Hormuz closure and plans to develop routes around the waterway during the Saudi leader’s two-day visit to Paris beginning Sunday, according to officials in the presidency who weren’t authorized to be publicly named.
Proposals under consideration include increasing trade through Omani ports outside the Persian Gulf, expanding or doubling pipelines in Saudi Arabia and elsewhere, and developing new rail links, the officials said.
France and Saudi Arabia have formed a task force on energy and logistics connections between the Middle East and Europe that is scheduled to meet at the ministerial level Monday.
The officials said the work was well advanced and would focus on identifying the most strategic projects, securing financing and establishing roles for French companies. The visit will be the crown prince’s first trip abroad since he traveled to Washington in November 2025, according to the officials.
— AP correspondent Angela Charlton in Paris

Trump: 'I view the strait of Hormuz as American territory'
Discussing the war with Iran at a South Carolina campaign event, Trump said: “I view the strait of Hormuz as an American territory right now. It’s an American territory.”
The president has faced scrutiny in recent days for making similar remarks as his administration struggles to end the war and gas prices reach record high levels. During a speech in New York last week, Trump said he would “pretty soon” designate the strait a US territory. The strait is a crucial waterway for global trade, bordered by Iran and Oman, and Tehran has refused to reopen it as peace talks continue to stall.
The president also recently claimed on social media that the US had “total control” over the strait, saying, “I think we will keep it.” Last week, Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, responded that Tehran would not be intimidated by the president’s threats and that the strait of Hormuz would only be opened under Iran’s authority.
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments:
Donald Trump thanked the supreme court for allowing work to proceed, for now, on what he has taken to calling his White House “Military/Ballroom Complex”. The president’s brief post was packed with misleading or false claims about the order and the ballroom he razed the entire East Wing of the White House to build.
Trump was asked if he could “guarantee that no tax money will be used in the construction of the ballroom?” The president replied, as he has for over a year, by insisting that the project would be entirely paid for by private donations, despite multiple reports that the project will drain hundreds of millions of taxpayer dollars from federal agencies.
The US Postal Service prepared to publish a final rule late on Friday to impose new requirements on states to provide the federal government with information on voters ahead of the November midterm congressional elections, despite a pair of court orders that currently block the changes from taking effect.
The Pentagon fired the publisher and editor in chief of Stars and Stripes, a US military news outlet partly funded by taxpayers, as well as a reporter after the outlet drew attention to dire conditions for service members fighting Iran.
Trump threatened a prominent progressive think tank, the Center for American Progress, with a $5bn lawsuit over its report that found the president’s expensive deployment of the national guard and other federal agents has done little to reduce violent crime in Washington DC and other cities.
US Postal Service posts new rule to alter mail-in voting in line with Trump's wishes, if courts allow it to proceed
The US Postal Service prepared to publish a final rule late on Friday to impose new requirements on states to provide the federal government with information on voters ahead of the November midterm congressional elections, despite a pair of court orders that currently block the changes from taking effect.
The USPS acknowledged in the text of the final rule posted online Friday, which is scheduled to be published in the Federal Register next week, that two injunctions issued by federal courts in California and Massachusetts currently bar it from moving ahead with the changes to comply with a March executive order signed by Donald Trump.
In accordance with the order, the postal service would require states to give the US Department of Homeland Security and other agencies access to lists of voters and to adopt new balloting procedures before the mail agency would make deliveries. If states did not comply, USPS would refuse to deliver the ballots.
Despite the injunctions, the Trump administration is pressing ahead with plans to disrupt votes cast by mail.
According to the text posted online Friday, the USPS is ready to implement the new restrictions on mail-in voting if the court injunctions are lifted.
If the government obtains timely relief from the injunctions, implementation immediately thereafter will provide election officials as much time as possible before the next election to comply with the rule’s preparation standards for Federal Ballot Mail envelopes, and to prepare to submit data to the Federal Ballot Mail Portal (“Portal”), before the mail-in and absentee ballots subject to this rule are mailed (which generally occurs in September or thereafter, as determined by state law). The Portal will become active (along with the verification process that relies on Portal data) at the time of the publication of the system of records (“SOR”) governing the Portal.
Nearly one in three Americans voted by mail in 2024, but Trump, who wants to restrict the number of voters by limiting ballots cast by mail, signed an executive order in March that prohibits the USPS from delivering ballots to any voters not on a federal list of citizens deemed eligible to vote in each state by the Department of Homeland Security.
The USPS proposal to implement this order seeks to require states to give the postal service the names and barcodes tied to mail-in ballots for federal elections. The service said it received more than 200,000 responses to its proposed rule change during a public comment period.
Trump himself voted by mail in Florida’s Republican primary this year, which was at least the third time the president has mailed his ballot.
Trump's South Carolina rally includes joke about bombing Iran
Trump has ended his campaign rally for Darline Graham in South Carolina after speaking for nearly 90 minutes, including joking about bombing Iran and recycling a decade-old complaint about Hillary Clinton.
At one point, the president asked the crowd if they wanted to hear him recite The Snake, a poem he used to frequently reference at campaign events about a woman who takes in a snake that later bites her. He said, “Do you want to hear The Snake? Look, it’s a Friday night. We have plenty of time, right? What the hell do I have to do? Go back, bomb Iran a little bit more?”
Trump also returned to an attack line against his 2016 revival, Hillary Clinton, mentioning her “deplorables” gaffe from ten years ago. In another moment, he brought up Karoline Leavitt, his press secretary who is stepping down and had a baby earlier this year.
“She just had a baby, and I just learned she loves the baby more than she loves Donald Trump, and I’m very angry with her,” the president said.
Trump was supporting Graham in advance of the Republican runoff on Tuesday to succeed her late brother, Lindsey. She is up against the ultra-conservative representative Ralph Norman and made headlines earlier this week when she stumbled during a debate and said, “I’m just going to be honest here. I’m not that informed on national security.”
A protester wearing a “kill your local pedophile” shirtwas ejected from a Trump rally in support of the South Carolina Senate campaign of Darline Graham, according to a Washington Examiner reporter at the event. The demonstrator also wore a hat with an upside down American flag.
The protester briefly interrupted a speech by the president, who has been delving into familiar campaign speech subjects, railing against “communist” Democrats and repeatedly returning to attacks on transgender people.
Trump: 'I view the strait of Hormuz as American territory'
Discussing the war with Iran at a South Carolina campaign event, Trump said: “I view the strait of Hormuz as an American territory right now. It’s an American territory.”
The president has faced scrutiny in recent days for making similar remarks as his administration struggles to end the war and gas prices reach record high levels. During a speech in New York last week, Trump said he would “pretty soon” designate the strait a US territory. The strait is a crucial waterway for global trade, bordered by Iran and Oman, and Tehran has refused to reopen it as peace talks continue to stall.
The president also recently claimed on social media that the US had “total control” over the strait, saying, “I think we will keep it.” Last week, Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, responded that Tehran would not be intimidated by the president’s threats and that the strait of Hormuz would only be opened under Iran’s authority.
Speaking at a campaign rally for Darline Graham in South Carolina, Trump is praising his poll numbers while also complaining about polls that reflect poorly on him:
Except for the fake polls out there, my poll numbers are great … they have such fake polls. So we have the greatest economy in our history. Now some people haven’t seen it yet, but they will, because the job numbers are so good … We have the greatest poll numbers that I’ve ever had. We have the greatest economy that I’ve ever had.”
A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found Americans preferred Democrats over Republicans as stewards of the economy for the first time in nearly a decade. That poll also found Americans’ approval of the president’s performance falling to 35%.
Trump touts his ballroom while rallying for Darline Graham
The president is now speaking at a rally in support of the Senate campaign of Darline Graham, the sister of the late senator, Lindsey Graham.
After a few minutes of praise for her campaign, Trump began discussing his ballroom project, saying he was in a “very good mood” after US supreme court chief justice John Roberts issued an order in his favor earlier today. The order allowed the White House to continue construction of the ballroom, a top Trump priority, while appeals challenging the project are ongoing.
At the rally, Trump described the ballroom as a “beautiful, magnificent complex, being built on the hallowed grounds of our cherished White House”. He said the ballroom was “so vital for national security” and would be “the greatest of its kind anywhere that’s ever been built”.
Trump shows reporters pro-Trump headlines from pro-Trump media
Concerns about the narrow, partisan nature of the media consumed by the president of the United States have spiked in recent days amid new attention to the role Donald Trump’s aide, Natalie Harp, plays in limiting what he sees, by printing out mainly flattering headlines and posts for him from the internet for him to read.
Trump himself accidentally offered up evidence of just how skewed his media diet is on Friday, when he used a few minutes with reporters to hold up a print-out of what he cast as important media headlines before boarding a flight to South Carolina for a rally in support of the Senate campaign of late Lindsey Graham’s sister, Darline.
“So, here are some headlines,” the president said after asking his press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, to hand him a print-out that displayed nine headlines, but no indiction of where they were published. “These are incredible headlines that just came out over the last 24 hours.”
“It’s probably easier if I show them to you than reading them,” Trump said, holding up the sheet of paper in front of photographers in the White House pool.
He then boasted about the headlines, which were largely taken from partisan, right-wing outlets that openly support him and simply repeated his administration’s claims.
Two of the headlines came from Breitbart, the far-right website its former editor Steve Bannon once described as a “platform for the alt-right”. Two came from outlets owned by Trump supporter Rupert Murdoch: the New York Post and Fox News. One was an opinion piece from a former Trump campaign spokesman published by the Daily Signal, a website founded by the Heritage Foundation, the right-wing think tank behind Project 2025. One came from Voz, a conservative news site aimed at Latinos founded in 2022 by pro-Trump executives.
The other three headlines came from avowedly non-partisan news outlets, Axios, CNN and the Washington Post, but in all three cases the headlines simply presented what looked like good news that the administration took credit.
As we reported last week, when Trump held up the Washington Post headline “Prescription drug prices record sharpest drop in more than 60 years”, the president apparently failed to read the article below, since it reported that independent experts actually attributed the price drop to Joe Biden, not Trump.
The secretary of the US Army, Dan Driscoll, is expected to step down from his role by the end of the year, after months of tension with the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday.
Driscoll, a friend and Yale Law school classmate of vice-president JD Vance, reportedly angered Hegseth near the very start of his tenure at the Pentagon when he offered to set up a visit by Vance and Donald Trump.
The departure, as the US is engaged in a war with Iran, would further deplete the US Army of Senate-confirmed leaders. In April, Hegseth fired the Army’s chief of staff, General Randy George and a replacement has yet to be nominated.
Trump again denies that taxpayers will fund his ballroom, despite evidence it will drain hundreds of millions from US budget
Speaking to reporters on his way to a political rally in South Carolina, Donald Trump was asked if he could “guarantee that no tax money will be used in the construction of the ballroom?”
The president replied, as he has for over a year, by insisting that the project would be entirely paid for by private donations, despite multiple reports that the project will drain hundreds of millions of taxpayer dollars from federal agencies.
“We’re spending hundreds of millions of dollars on the ballroom and it’s all from people like me and great companies that are putting it up. It’s going to be close to $400 million and it’s all paid for by patriots and patriotic companies,” Trump said. “No taxpayer money for the ballroom at all.”
But the Washington Post reported in June that Trump’s claim is simply untrue. A project summary prepared by the ballroom contractor obtained by the Post showed that the total construction was expected to cost $600m, with more than half of the funds coming from taxpayers.
Two days later, the New York Times revealed that the Trump administration had shifted over $350m from the Secret Service’s budget to White House to pay for a secure military bunker underneath the luxury ballroom.
Trump thanks supreme court for allowing work to proceed on his 'Military/Ballroom Complex'
In a social media post on Friday, Donald Trump thanked the supreme court for allowing work to proceed, for now, on what he has taken to calling his White House “Military/Ballroom Complex”.
The president’s brief post was packed with misleading or false claims about the order and the ballroom he razed the entire East Wing of the White House to start building.
“We are grateful for the Decision of the United States Supreme Court”, Trump wrote, mischaracterizing the single-sentence order from one justice, John Roberts, as a decision of the court. In fact, Roberts only lifted a preliminary injunction from a lower court that had blocked above-ground work on the ballroom to give the full supreme court time to reach a final decision on whether the president can complete the project.
“The Military/Ballroom Complex being built on the hallowed grounds of the White House, which is so vital for National Security, will be THE GREATEST OF ITS KIND!” Trump continued, continuing to cast the creation of a vast reception hall on the White House grounds as somehow motivated by a concern to increase security around the presidential residence.
A White House bunker beneath the East Wing, demolished by Trump in his rush to construct his ballroom, does need to be replaced, but he is simply solving a problem he created. Trump was reportedly rushed into the bunker by the Secret Service in 2020, as protesters rallied to decry police violence against Black Americans after the murder of George Floyd.
“It is something that Presidents have wanted for 150 years, and that the Military has been seeking for the last 100 years,” Trump continued, repeating an entirely unsourced claim he has been making for more than a year now.
“Their wish will soon be fulfilled! Construction is under budget and ahead of schedule,” he concluded. Although this is a claim Trump has been making about building projects since his days as a real estate developer, it is clearly not true that construction of the ballroom is “under budget” given that the White House first said the ballroom would cost approximately $200m when it was unveiled in July 2025, before the president started calling if a $400m project, and the contractor hired for the ballroom reportedly told the White House in March that the project cost had soared to $600m, according to a document obtained by the Washington Post.
Senator Chuck Schumer, who leads the Democratic minority in the Senate, denounced the supreme court order Trump hailed.
“The MAGA Supreme Court is rubber stamping Trump’s vanity-driven, gilded corruption,” Schumer posted in response to the news.
“As costs skyrocket, the administration is wasting money on an endless and illegal war, corporate giveaways, and Trump’s pet projects,” Schumer added. “We will continue to fight this flagrant waste of taxpayer money relentlessly in the courts.”
Stars and Stripes editor says he has been fired for insubordination after doing interview
In an update to my earlier post, the Pentagon is confirmed to have fired the editor-in-chief of Stars and Stripes, Erik Slavin, as well as its publisher, Max Lederer, and a reporter, Slavin has told the Associated Press.
Slavin said he was dismissed for insubordination after an interview he gave that objected to any potential censorship by the US military.
He told the AP he was fired “for stating in a CBS interview that hypothetical censorship of news for service members would constitute a red line”. He added that he stands by the principle “that Stars and Stripes must remain editorially independent”.
Earlier this week, Lederer announced his retirement effective at the end of September. He too received a separation notice, according to Slavin, as did the Middle East reporter Lara Korte.
Trump threatens think tank with $5bn lawsuit over report that found 'no evidence' that his national guard deployments had affected crime rate
The New York Times (paywall) reports that Donald Trump has threatened a prominent progressive think tank with a $5bn lawsuit over a report that found the president’s expensive deployment of the national guard and other federal agents has done little to reduce violent crime in Washington DC and other cities.
Trump regularly touts his supposed success in taking DC “from high crime to no crime”. For instance, a few weeks ago he told reporters in the Oval Office: “This was the crime capital, frankly, of the world. It was the most unsafe capital of any country in the world. Now, it’s one of the safest, and it’s one of the safest places in the United States.”
Last month, the Center for American Progress published findings that Trump’s deployments had failed to reduce violent crime despite its claims of success. The analysis highlighted that violent crime rates had already dropped before Trump took office again, and said his administration “is using these declines to justify expanding policies that are unpopular, ineffective, and costly”.
It’s summary reads:
Even though the data clearly show that violent crime and homicides were already dropping in American cities in 2023 and 2024, the Trump administration has continued to threaten city and state leaders and argue that its extreme actions, such as deploying the National Guard to support law enforcement operations, are improving public safety.
However, new Center for American Progress analysis finds no evidence that National Guard deployments have reduced violent crime. Moreover, if these deployments are extended and continue through the end of 2026, they could cost American taxpayers more than $1.7 billion.
This left the administration displeased. Per the NYT’s report:
On Monday, one of Mr. Trump’s personal lawyers, Alejandro Brito, wrote a letter to the center warning that he would file the suit if the group did not fully retract the report, which was published on its website on July 13. The letter, viewed by The New York Times, was addressed to the group’s president and chief executive, Neera Tanden, a longtime Democratic official who served as a senior adviser to President Joseph R. Biden Jr., and to several of its board members.
Mr. Brito claimed that the report about the National Guard was full of malicious and false statements. He gave Ms. Tanden and members of her board until 5 p.m. on Friday to retract it and apologize to Mr. Trump.
Tanden hit back, telling the Times in a statement that the center would “neither cower nor bend in the face” of legal action. She also defended the report, asserting that while its findings might have been “inconvenient to the Trump administration”, they were “grounded in rigorous, evidence-based research and analysis”.
She added:
This threatened lawsuit’s attack on facts and evidence is baseless.A fundamental protection of the First Amendment is to allow for the publication of facts and analysis that is contrary to the arguments and claims of any administration.A lawsuit is a transparent attempt to silence us.
Pentagon moves to fire publisher and editor of Stars and Stripes - report
The Pentagon has moved to fire both the publisher and the editor in chief of Stars and Stripes, the leading US military news outlet partly funded by taxpayers, for alleged insubordination, CBS News reports.
Separation notices were delivered today, and give publisher Max Lederer and editor-in-chief Erik Slavin five days to appeal their dismissals, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke to CBS News. The cause cited was insubordination, one of the people said. They did not elaborate on the details of the alleged insubordination.
Lederer, the publisher of the military daily for 19 years, had this week told colleagues he planned to retire on 30 September, citing fundamental differences with the Trump administration.
“It has become clear that my philosophy of leadership, and my understanding of value and mission of the Stars and Stripes, differ in fundamental ways from the direction of the leadership of the Department of Defense,” Lederer said in a letter to staff, which was posted on X.
This comes days after the outlet revealed, along with the Navy Times, the deteriorating conditions and mental health crisis for service members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, which is on a record-breaking nine-month deployment in the Middle East as part of the US-Israel war on Iran.
It is unclear whether that reporting is linked to the reported discussions inside the Pentagon. But Slavin has spoken publicly about disagreements with Pentagon leaders.
As my colleague Edward Helmore notes, Slavin hinted at tensions with the military brass just last month when he said the “foxhole” he would be willing to die in would be over editorial independence from the Pentagon, which provides about 65% of its funding.
Earlier this year, the Pentagon spokesperson, Sean Parnell, posted on X: “We are bringing Stars & Stripes into the 21st century. We will modernize its operations, refocus its content away from woke distractions that syphon morale, and adapt it to serve a new generation of service members.”
Further to our earlier posts on the backlash over reports that a navy aircraft carrier set to honor a Black war hero may, instead, be named after Donald Trump, it seems worth noting that in Trump’s executive order last week, when he demanded that a new aircraft carrier under construction be redesigned to install steam catapults to launch fighter jets, there was no mention of the fact that the ship was to be named the USS Doris Miller, in honor of a Black hero of Pearl Harbor. The order did not refer to the ship at any point as the USS Miller, a name chosen by the navy during Trump’s first term, but instead used just the ship’s hull number, CVN-81.
Supreme court chief justice allows work on Trump’s $400m White House ballroom to continue for now
Chief Justice John Roberts is allowing the White House to continue construction on Donald Trump’s controversial $400m ballroom project for now, the Associated Press reports, as the supreme court considers the Trump administration’s emergency request to intervene in lawsuits over the project.
The brief, one-page document does not detail Roberts’ reasoning or lay out a timeline for a fuller decision from the high court.
Lower courts had ordered a halt to the project, finding that it must have congressional approval. That ruling was set to take effect today.
When Trump first announced the plans for a new ballroom, he did not emphasize national security.
He also said the project would be funded by private donations, including from himself. But in June it was revealed that the administration had quietly redirected $352m in federal funds designated for the Secret Service toward the project, after Congress explicitly refused to provide $1bn in funds for it.
Migrants reportedly flown to Equatorial Guinea after resisting Liberia deportation under Trump deal
Five people whom the US attempted to deport to Liberia this week resisted getting off the plane and were instead transported to Equatorial Guinea, another African country to which the Trump administration is removing migrants it cannot legally send home, two sources familiar with the matter have told Reuters.
The incident represents an early snag in Washington’s plan to send up to 1,200 so-called third-country deportees to Liberia, one of the largest such deals it has struck in Africa despite criticism from immigrants’ rights advocates.
Third-country deportees have, in most cases, obtained legal protection against repatriation after US immigration judges ruled they risked torture or other abuses in their home countries.
Liberia announced on Tuesday that it had agreed to receive deportees and that the first group of 20 would arrive on Thursday. But a Liberian official, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter, told Reuters today that only 15 deportees disembarked.
At least five others - three Cuban men, one Brazilian man and one Cameroonian woman - refused to get off the plane in Liberia, according to three sources familiar with the incident, one of whom was a Honduran deportee on the flight.
Authorities then told them they would be flown to the US, but the plane instead headed to Malabo, in Equatorial Guinea, where the five were forced to disembark against their will, two of the sources said.
Liberia’s information ministry did not respond to a Reuters request for comment on Friday.
The five are now being held with more than 30 other migrants whom the Trump administration had previously sent to Equatorial Guinea under a deal that, like others in Africa, has been denounced by human rights groups and advocates who say many of the deportees are ultimately repatriated.
In May, human rights experts at the United Nations issued a rare public appeal to Equatorial Guinea, urging the country to halt its plans to return US deportees to their home countries, where they face political violence, torture and death.
The US state department said it remained “unwavering in our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration and bolster America’s border security”.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said all the migrants “were deported to a safe third country”, adding: “If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them. Period.”
Thomas Bledsoe told CNN the potential move is “quite a shock” and that the family were not notified beforehand. “Not only was it a shock, but it was also shocking that we found out from a new outlet [and not] from the Navy,” he said.
But this isn’t just about a name on a ship, he added.
It’s about an opportunity and a goal. It’s about what it means to be an American and it’s also about how we as a community can grow as one.
