articles.title: Former Air Force Secretary James G. Roche Dies at 86
articles.body:
James G. Roche, the 20th Secretary of the Air Force who led the department from 2001-2005, died Aug. 4. He was 86.
As Secretary, Roche led the Air Force through the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks and subsequent preparations and campaigns in Afghanistan in 2001 and Iraq in 2003. During his tenure, he pushed for tighter synergy between the Air Force’s air and space activities, improved readiness, a shift from platform-based acquisition to capabilities- and networks-based systems, and setting the Air Force on a course to adopt combat drones partnered with piloted aircraft; a concept now coming to fruition in the form of Collaborative Combat Aircraft.
Though nominated by President George W. Bush to be Army Secretary in 2005, Roche withdrew his name from consideration when it became apparent that congressional opponents would block his confirmation indefinitely. At issue was Roche’s promotion of a plan to replace the Air Force’s oldest aerial tankers with aircraft leased from Boeing. One of Roche’s acquisition officials acted improperly in pursuit of the idea: that official went to jail and another resigned, but Roche himself was not found to have acted criminally.
Born in Brooklyn, N.Y., in 1939, Roche earned a bachelor’s degree in humanities from Chicago’s Illinois Institute of Technology in 1960 and took up a Navy commission through the ROTC. In 1966 he completed a master’s in operations research from the Navy postgraduate school in Monterey, Calif. , and earned a doctorate in business administration from Harvard in 1972.
Roche served 23 years as a Navy officer, during which he commanded the guided missile destroyer USS Buchanan. While in uniform, he worked on the Senate intelligence committee and served as deputy to Andrew Marshall, the Pentagon’s Director of Net Assessment. Retiring as a captain in 1983, he then headed the Democratic staff of the Senate Armed Services Committee for a year, moving to Northrop in 1984. He headed the company’s analysis center in Washington for five years, then became a vice president and assistant to Northrop CEO Tom Jones. A series of executive positions with Northrop followed: first as VP and then chief of advanced development and planning, then as president of Northrop’s Electronic Sensors and Systems sector until his appointment by Bush to be Air Force Secretary in 2001.
In the months leading up to the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, Roche moved to enhance the appeal and quality of life for enlisted Airmen by improving their educational opportunities and living conditions. He insisted the Air Force’s air and space capabilities needed to be more closely aligned: he set in motion plans to integrate air- and space-based sensor and communications networks, and expanded the integration of space capabilities with field units. He also moved to improve readiness through more exercises and more funding for spare parts.
Roche also took a cue from Chief of Staff Gen. John Jumper to pursue unmanned combat aircraft. In 2000, Jumper, as head of Air Combat Command, had directed the arming of MQ-9 Predator reconnaissance drones, tests of which began in early 2001. Roche saw armed, self-directed drones as certain to be an important part of the Air Force’s future. He began to promote the idea—pushing for further development of experiments like the X-45 Unmanned Combat Aircraft Vehicle, already underway—and in several speeches and internal messages told Air Force leaders to anticipate and begin preparing for the day when unmanned combat aerial vehicles, or UCAVs, would fly alongside piloted aircraft or pursue combat missions independently.
While successful, the UCAV experiment did not become a top Air Force acquisition priority until Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall formally started the CCA program in 2022. It is likely the Air Force’s UCAV program transitioned to classified efforts in the intervening years. Roche frequently touted combat UAVs as assets that did not tire and could undertake long missions without degraded “acuity.” He also noted that if a drone is lost in combat, “you don’t have to write a letter to the mother of a computer chip.”
In the immediate aftermath of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, Roche put greater emphasis on the Air Expeditionary Forces concept, already then taking shape, pumping more people, aircraft, and logistical backing into the construct, and shifting emphasis from stateside garrison activities to forward deployments. He pushed the deployment of unmanned aircraft like the RQ-4 Global Hawk and MQ-1 Predator into the Southwest Asia theater, even though both were still considered experimental. Along with the Army, he fostered greater field cooperation between the services, putting airmen in Army ground units to facilitate air attacks and close air support.
Roche also increased the use of the Air National Guard and Air Force Reserve in the Afghanistan campaign, integrating those units more closely with the Active-Duty force; leading to a day-to-day operational dependency on reserves that the Air Force still maintains.
In addition, Roche advocated creation of more Air Operations Centers as a way to develop Air Force and joint networks and integrated capabilities, and moved to add more Air Force special operations capabilities to aid the other services.
Soon after 9/11, Roche was favorably inclined toward a plan suggested Sen. Ted Stevens (R-Alaska) to rapidly obtain additional aerial refueling capability by leasing such aircraft from Boeing, which had built the KC-135 and KC-10 tankers. The idea was that leasing the aircraft would allow them to be acquired through operations and maintenance accounts rather than through an outright acquisition program at a time when the Air Force was strapped for modernization dollars. It was also thought that a lease would bring the jets online faster than a straight buy. For his part, Stevens saw the idea as a way to help prop up Boeing and the U.S. airline industry, which had taken a body blow in canceled orders due to the terrorist attacks, which had caused a precipitous drop in air travel.
Roche favored quickly awarding a contract to Boeing both as a boost to the U.S. industrial base and because Boeing alone had a recent design for a boom-type refueling system. However, European airliner maker Airbus/EADS persuaded members of Congress that it could quickly certify its own boom and create a production line in the U.S. and should be allowed to compete for the work. Those members and others succeeded in getting the Air Force to agree to a “best value” competition, since EADS could not compete on unit price alone, given that its A330 aircraft was much larger than Boeing’s 767-based tanker.
In emails that came to light through subsequent investigations, it was clear that Roche favored a sole-source Boeing approach. He also had a personal animosity toward Ralph Crosby—a former Northrop rival—who was then head of EADS North America. Roche disparaged EADS’s offering of the Airbus A330 tanker as a mostly European product with only a “Made in America” sticker on it.
Roche also reportedly had an ongoing feud with Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) dating back to their Navy days, and McCain, a powerful voice on the Senate Armed Services Committee, made the tanker lease a personal crusade, publicly criticizing it as a “sweetheart deal” for Boeing that would cost the government far more than a straight purchase. He demanded numerous investigations of the plan.
Darleen Druyun, who had been the Air Force’s Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary for Acquisition and Management for 10 years, was zealous in promoting the Boeing lease. Several investigations determined that Druyun passed information to Boeing about EADS’ proposal and had demanded from Boeing an executive job for herself and jobs for other family members in exchange for giving Boeing favorable terms on the lease and overall favorable treatment on the competition. She also collaborated with Boeing to give the company favorable terms on launch vehicle contracts and steered the initial Small Diameter Bomb contract to the company. Druyun was arrested and eventually served nine months in prison, but it was determined Roche had not directed her to commit the contracting crimes and was unaware of her activities. One Boeing executive also went to jail and longtime Boeing CEO Phil Condit resigned. Boeing had to pay a $615 million fine. Druyun’s immediate boss, Marvin Sambur, resigned his post, but was not found to have participated in Druyun’s scheme.
McCain and other Senators held up promotions of several senior Air Force officers while demanding information and awaiting investigation results on the tanker lease, which the Air Force finally abandoned in fall 2004. Instead, it decided to buy 100 tankers, but that plan went through extensive modifications and reruns of a competition until Boeing was finally awarded a contract in 2011 for 179 KC-46 tankers.
Soon after the lease plan imploded, Bush nominated Roche to take on the post of Secretary of the Army, but he withdrew his name from nomination when it became clear his confirmation would be blocked indefinitely by tanker foes in Congress. He said it was unfair to make the senior officers awaiting promotion to wait while his issues were resolved. He announced his resignation from the Air Force in November 2004, and departed the job at the beginning of the second Bush term, in January 2005. Roche said he had always planned on serving only one term and allowed some overlap of his successor with the term of Gen. John Jumper.
Roche himself was found to have committed an ethics violation by sending an email recommending a person for a job with Northrop. While the recommendation itself wasn’t an ethical violation, Roche’s use of his official email, which bore his government title and potentially implied government endorsement, constituted the infraction. Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld considered the mistake inadvertent and did not pursue any sanctions.
In retirement, Roche served on the board of Orbital Sciences Corp./Orbital ATK until it became part of Northrop Grumman. He was also a member of the Council on Foreign Relations and the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
Ret. Lt. Gen. David Deptula, head of AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, worked for Roche during the Air Force’s 2001 Quadrennial Defense Review.
“Secretary Roche’s impact on our national security cannot be overstated,” Deptula said. “Whether in uniform, in industry, or as Secretary of the Air Force, he was a most innovative, dedicated, and driven individual. He didn’t simply receive briefings—he understood the issues at a fundamental level, challenged assumptions, and pressed those of us on his staff to advance our thinking about air and space power. His command of strategy and policy, coupled with his deep interest in science and technology, was second to none. He made the Air Force and the nation stronger, and had a significant impact as a result.”
Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach wrote on social media that Roche “led our Department … through one of its most consequential moments following September 11th, cementing air and space power as the linchpin of the Joint Force.”
The current Secretary of the Air Force, Troy Meink, wrote that Roche’s “leadership and commitment helped strengthen the Joint Force, leaving a true impression on our nation.”

articles.title: Israel struck Syrian base despite being told no Turkish troops: Barrack
articles.body:
Israel’s unannounced airstrike on a Syrian airbase near Türkiye’s border created a serious risk of military miscalculation between the two countries, U.S. Ambassador to Türkiye and special envoy for Syria Tom Barrack has said.
In an interview with PBS NewsHour on Aug. 21, Barrack said Israeli aircraft approached to within about 80 kilometers of Türkiye’s border without Ankara receiving advance notice.
He said Israel had told Washington and Damascus for the preceding five days that it was concerned Türkiye might place military personnel or equipment at Abu al-Duhur airbase in northwestern Syria.
Washington consulted its intelligence agencies, while Syrian officials told Mossad that no Turkish troops, convoy or weapons were at the facility and that no hostile activity was underway, according to Barrack.
The sides expected the dialogue to continue, but Israel struck the base on Aug. 18, damaging its runways.
“The attack was unannounced,” Barrack said, adding that “avoiding kinetic interaction or surprises is the goal.”
In a separate Reuters interview after the strike, Barrack said Türkiye saw aircraft flying north toward its territory and could “reasonably have prepared its own response.”
“Thankfully, calm heads were able to prevent the situation from deteriorating further,” he said.
Barrack said Washington understood Israel’s security concerns but had seen no hostile or aggressive move by Türkiye or Syria.
He urged Israel to address its concerns through direct or back-channel talks with Ankara instead of unilateral military action.
Israel acknowledged the strike after Barrack described it as an “unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability.”
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the operation was intended to prevent a Turkish troop deployment and accused Syria of nearing a breach of what Israel described as a security status quo.
Both Ankara and Damascus have denied plans to establish a Turkish base or permanent military presence at Abu al-Duhur.
Türkiye’s Defense Ministry said no Turkish military delegation was at the base before or during the attack.
It also said Ankara would continue supporting Syria’s efforts to rebuild its infrastructure and military capacity under the principle of “one state, one army.”
Türkiye and Syria signed a memorandum on joint military training and consultancy on Aug. 13, 2025.
Turkish officials have said its implementation covers training, consultancy, technical assistance and reciprocal visits aimed at strengthening Syria’s defense capacity.
Türkiye says its assistance is provided at the request of the Syrian government and is intended to reinforce the country’s unity, territorial integrity and ability to combat terrorism.
Rhetoric between Türkiye and Israel intensified on Aug. 21 after Netanyahu’s office directed accusations to President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.
Türkiye’s Communications Directorate rejected the remarks as lacking “historical facts and political seriousness” and accused the Israeli government of portraying Türkiye as a threat for electoral gain.
Barrack said much of the hostile rhetoric was political and noted that Israel was in an election cycle.
He called for lower tensions and a return to dialogue.

articles.title: Middle East live: Iran allows several Iraqi oil tankers to pass through Hormuz strait
articles.body:
Iran has allowed a number of Iraqi oil tankers to pass through the Strait of Hormuz following repeated requests from Baghdad, Iran’s state news agency reported on Saturday. Meanwhile, the United States and Iran exchanged defiant messages ahead of Monday's scheduled announcement of new US economic sanctions. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
Dozens of UK, French ex-ambassadors accuse Israel of ethnic cleansing in open letter
Former British and French diplomats are urging action over what they say is Israel’s "erasure"of Palestine. More than 100 of those diplomats have penned a letter to the French President and the British Prime Minister calling for a ban on trade and arms sales to press Israel to accept a Palestinian state.
FRANCE 24 speaks to one of the signatories – Sir Vincent Fean, British former Consul-General Jerusalem and current trustee of the Britain Palestine Project to understand what does he hope the letter will achieve?
Iranian official urges Qatar to move detained pilots to hospital on land, Tasnim says
An Iranian military official called on Qatar on Saturday to transfer detained Iranian pilots to a hospital on land, saying they were being held on water and were in "poor physical condition", Tasnim news agency reported.
Mohammad Baqerzadeh, commander of the Committee for the Search for Missing Persons of Iran's Armed Forces General Staff, said the location where the pilots were being held was unsuitable and requested that the International Committee of the Red Cross send an air ambulance to Qatar to expedite the return of injured and sick detainees to Iran.
Repair of Iran's South Pars phase 14 refinery is 70% complete, state news agency says
The repair of Iran's South Pars Phase 14 gas refinery, hit during an Israeli attack in June last year, is 70% complete, the Pars Oil and Gas Company's chief executive said, according to Iran's oil ministry news agency SHANA.
The refinery would be fully restored by the end of the year, CEO Touraj Dehqani said, and the damaged section will be fully integrated into the production cycle, he added.
Israel says US criticism of strike on Syria 'full of inaccuracies'

Katz wrote on X that Israel had passed on "intelligence information to the authorised parties in the United States" before the strike, and that Barrack's comment was "full of inaccuracies and positions that contradict the stance of US President (Donald) Trump himself regarding the Golan Heights".
Syria condemns Israeli strike as 'flagrant violation of sovereignty'
Syria condemned an Israeli strike southwest of Damascus that wounded one person on Saturday, the second such attack in a week.
"This attack constitutes a flagrant violation of the sovereignty of the Syrian Arab Republic and the integrity of its territory, and a blatant breach of international law, and comes in the context of repeated Israeli attacks on Syrian territory," the foreign ministry said in a statement.

US and Iran keep up hostile rhetoric ahead of new sanctions
The United States and Iran exchanged defiant messages ahead of Monday's scheduled announcement of new US economic sanctions that could impact the Islamic Republic and Tehran's most important trading partners including China.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Saturday that the imminent US announcement of new economic sanctions on Iran was an "assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty over every independent member state of the United Nations."
US President Donald Trump, who has warned of economic consequences against any country that provides "any type of lifeline to Iran," said on Friday that Washington was observing "what happens" in the conflict.

Iran grants permission for Iraqi oil tankers to pass through Strait of Hormuz,
Iran has granted permission for a number of Iraqi oil tankers to pass through the Strait of Hormuz following repeated requests from Baghdad through various channels, Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported on Saturday.

US President Donald Trump said he did not think that Iran was ready make the "right deal", and that Washington was observing "what happens" in the conflict.

articles.title: Who Is Lev Shlosberg, the Russian Politician Jailed for Opposing Russia’s War?
articles.body:
Russia has sentenced Lev Shlosberg, the 63-year-old deputy chairman of the liberal Yabloko party – and one of the few prominent opponents of Russia’s war against Ukraine who chose to remain in the country – to 11 years and one month in a penal colony for participating in a debate and reposting a newspaper cover.
On Aug. 17, a court in the northwestern city of Pskov found him guilty of repeatedly “discrediting” the Russian military and spreading “false information” about it. The court also prohibited him from administering websites for six years,Reuters reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
On the same day, Russia’s Supreme Court rejected Yabloko’s appeal against its exclusion from the Sept. 18-20 parliamentary election. Yabloko was the only registered Russian party openly campaigning for an end to the war.
The two rulings removed both an anti-war party from the ballot and one of its best-known politicians from public life. Dozens of people who gathered near the Supreme Court were detained.
Eleven years for a debate and a repost
One part of the case concerned Shlosberg’s January 2025 online debate with historian Yuri Pivovarov.
Shlosberg argued that Russia and Ukraine should agree to an immediate ceasefire. Pivovarov warned that a premature settlement could produce another war and supported Ukraine fighting until victory.
Investigators claimed that a recording of the debate posted on the Russian social network Odnoklassniki “discredited” the military. Shlosberg said he did not control the account and had not uploaded the recording.
Russian Emigration Interest Doubles Amid Fears of Mobilization This Fall
The second charge concerned a repost from Feb. 25, 2022 – the day after Russia launched its full-scale invasion. It showed a Daily Mirror front page featuring an injured Ukrainian woman alongside Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
The law criminalizing “false information” about the Russian military was signed on March 4, after the repost had already appeared. The court nevertheless used the publication to help impose a sentence of more than 11 years.
The proceedings were troubling even by the standards of a Russian political trial. According to Deutsche Welle, closing arguments began without any of Shlosberg’s three lawyers present. The court refused to postpone the hearing and imposed a state-appointed lawyer whom he had rejected.
The sentence incorporated an earlier punishment of 420 hours of compulsory labor for allegedly failing to comply with the requirements imposed on a so-called “foreign agent.”
Amnesty International called the prosecution retaliation for exercising freedom of expression. Human Rights Watch demanded his release and noted that the offending “false information” included the image of a wounded Ukrainian civilian.
Pskov politician who investigated Russia’s secret war
Shlosberg was born in Pskov in 1963 into a family of teachers. He studied history at the Pskov Pedagogical Institute, later worked as a teacher and social worker, and helped establish the non-state Pskov Free Institute in the early 1990s, according to a biographical account published while he was in pretrial detention.
He joined Yabloko in 1994 and led its Pskov branch from 1996 until 2023, when he became one of the party’s deputy chairs.
Unlike opposition figures whose careers were made in Moscow, Shlosberg built his reputation through local politics, journalism and civic work. He was twice elected to the Pskov Regional Assembly, first serving from 2011 to 2015 and then from 2016 to 2021.
He was also the publisher and editor of Pskovskaya Guberniya, a regional newspaper whose reporting brought him national attention, and nearly cost him his life.
In August 2014, while the Kremlin denied that regular Russian troops were fighting in eastern Ukraine, the newspaper investigated the funerals of service members from Pskov’s 76th Guards Air Assault Division.
The soldiers had officially died in unclear circumstances. The evidence indicated that they had been killed during Russia’s undeclared intervention in the Donbas.
The issue was particularly sensitive in Pskov. The division was one of the region’s most important military institutions, and reporting on its losses punctured Moscow’s claim that the war was a purely Ukrainian conflict involving local “separatists” and Russian volunteers.
On Aug. 29, 2014, unknown assailants attacked Shlosberg near his home. He was hospitalized with a concussion, facial injuries and temporary memory loss. The assault followed a wider series of threats and attacks on journalists trying to establish how Russian soldiers had died in Ukraine, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists.
No one was held accountable for the attack.
In 2015, fellow regional deputies stripped Shlosberg of his mandate after he represented a civic organization contesting its designation as a “foreign agent.” He considered the decision political retaliation. The following year, he received the inaugural Boris Nemtsov Prize for his defense of democratic values and returned to the regional assembly in an election.
Opposition to Crimea seizure
Shlosberg opposed Russia’s seizure of Crimea from the beginning. In a 2016 essay titled “The Crimean Dead End,” he described how Russian troops blockaded Ukrainian military facilities before a referendum held under occupation.
Yabloko’s subsequent election platform stated that Crimea belonged to Ukraine, that its annexation was illegal and that it should be reversed. This was an unusually direct position for a party still permitted to operate legally in Russia.
After the full-scale invasion began, Shlosberg continued to oppose the war publicly. He described the war as a game of “bloody chess” and argued that peace had to precede political change.
“We must first stop killing people,” he said in the debate that later became part of his criminal case. “If we achieve peace, we will regain freedom.”
The repression accumulated gradually.
Russian courts repeatedly fined Shlosberg and his wife, Zhanna, for allegedly “discrediting” the military. In June 2023, the Justice Ministry designated him a “foreign agent,” a label used to stigmatize critics and exclude them from political life.
In 2024, he was fined for reposting Arnold Schwarzenegger’s March 2022 appeal to Russians about the war. Authorities searched his home and the home of his elderly father.
In June 2025, he was detained over the debate with Pivovarov and placed under house arrest. When investigators opened the separate “false information” case in December, he was transferred to pretrial detention, where he remained until his conviction.
Despite other prominent anti-Putin figures like Maxim Katz, Shlosberg refused to leave Russia and compared himself to Antaeus, the figure from Greek mythology who lost his strength when separated from the earth.
Anti-war position that Ukrainians strongly disputed
Despite Shlosberg’s opposition to some of the Kremlin’s actions, his stance toward Russia’s war on Ukraine still raises an eyebrow.
His position after the full-scale invasion centered on a form of radical pacifism and an immediate, unconditional ceasefire. In a December 2024 Yabloko essay, he argued that shooting should stop first and questions of territory, borders, sanctions and European security should be negotiated afterward.
For Ukrainians, the problem is obvious. A ceasefire that does not require Russian withdrawal may freeze an occupation achieved through aggression, give Moscow time to rearm and leave millions of Ukrainians under Russian rule.
That year he also made another controversial statement. He argued that Ukraine ceased to be a victim when it began resisting, saying that the “myth that Ukraine remains a victim” did not correspond to history.
After Ukraine’s operation in Russia’s Kursk region, he attacked exiled Russian opposition figures who supported Kyiv and called them the “party of other people’s blood.” Critics accused him of focusing on Ukrainian military action while failing to recognize Ukraine’s right to strike the forces and infrastructure used to attack it.
Why the Kremlin chose this moment
Four and a half year into the full-scale war, the Kremlin has tightened its grip on all opposition. Even parties without wide support like Yabloko.
Shlosberg’s Fellow Yabloko deputy chair Maxim Kruglov was also sentenced to seven years in June for allegedly spreading “false information” about the military. Other party members have been imprisoned, declared “foreign agents” or excluded from elections.
On Aug. 10, the Supreme Court removed Yabloko from the ballot following a complaint by the ultranationalist Rodina party. A week later, the court rejected Yabloko’s appeal while Shlosberg was being sentenced in Pskov.
In his final statement, Shlosberg called the war a catastrophe and warned that Russia would eventually have to confront the full list of its dead. He said military cemeteries were expanding faster than maternity wards, kindergartens and schools.
The judge repeatedly interrupted him, and in the end granted the 11 year sentence that epitomizes modern Russia’s zeitgeist: that of a state edging on totalitarianism as the Russian authorities continue to ban social media, interfere with the private lives of its citizens, and silence all criticism.

articles.title: Russia Conducted Missile Drills Near Kuril Islands Following Putin’s Visit and Protests by Japan
articles.body:
Russia conducted high-profile missile exercises near the Southern Kuril Islands after Japan lodged a protest over Vladimir Putin’s visit to the occupied island of Iturup.
The Ministry of Defence of the Russian Federation announced the exercises.
During the exercises, the Russian Pacific Fleet deployed a strike group consisting of the missile cruiser Varyag, the nuclear submarine Omsk, and the Bastion coastal missile system.
As part of the exercises, the cruiser Varyag fired two Vulcan anti-ship missiles, and the submarine Omsk launched a Granit cruise missile.
In addition, the crew of the Bastion coastal missile system, deployed on one of the islands, fired an Onyx anti-ship missile.
Russia has been strengthening its military presence in the Kuril Islands for quite some time.
As early as November 2016, the Pacific Fleet’s newspaper Boevaya Vakhta reported on the deployment of the Bal and Bastion coastal anti-ship missile systems on the islands of Iturup and Kunashir.
And in 2021, Russia deployed the Bastion coastal anti-ship missile system on Matua Island.
In late 2017, the Russian military also completed the restoration of an airfield on the island and announced plans to establish a base there for Russian Navy ships.
The Southern Kuril Islands are under Russian control, but Japan considers them its Northern Territories. Tokyo has consistently opposed the strengthening of Russia’s military presence on these islands.
The Japanese prime minister then called the Russian president’s visit ‘absolutely unacceptable.’
The missile drills took place against the backdrop of a new escalation in relations between Moscow and Tokyo. Russian President Vladimir Putin recently visited Iturup Island, prompting protests from Japan.
The territorial dispute over the Kuril Islands has been ongoing for more than 80 years, ever since the Soviet Union established control over the four islands. Japan claims them and demands their return, while Russia considers the islands its territory. Due to this unresolved issue, Moscow and Tokyo have yet to sign a full-fledged peace treaty following the war.

articles.title: russia attacked Ukraine with 217 attack drones and missiles - air defense destroyed 191 targets
articles.body:
russia attacked Ukraine with 217 attack drones and missiles - air defense destroyed 191 targets
Kyiv • UNN
Russia struck Ukraine with missiles, munitions, and 217 drones. Air defense destroyed or suppressed 191 targets; hits were recorded at 41 locations.
During the night of August 22, Russia attacked Ukraine with ballistic and air-launched missiles, loitering munitions, and 217 attack drones. At the same time, Ukrainian air defense shot down or suppressed 191 enemy targets. The main areas targeted were the Kyiv and Odesa regions. This is reported by the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, UNN reports.
Details
During the night of August 22 (from 18:00 on August 21), the enemy attacked Ukraine with missiles that approach their targets along a ballistic trajectory—Iskander-M and S-400 missiles—as well as three Kh-31P/Kh-59 air-launched missiles from the Kursk, Bryansk, and Belgorod regions and from the airspace over the waters of the Black Sea. It also used "Banderol" loitering munitions and 217 Shahed-type attack UAVs (more than 50 of them jet-powered), Gerbera UAVs, and "Parody"-type decoy drones launched from the following directions: Kursk, Oryol, Millerovo, Primorsko-Akhtarsk — Russian Federation; the temporarily occupied Donetsk; and Hvardiiske — the temporarily occupied Autonomous Republic of Crimea
According to the agency, the main areas targeted were the Kyiv and Odesa regions. The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 09:00, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed three Kh-31P/Kh-59 air-launched missiles, six "Banderol" loitering munitions, as well as 182 enemy UAVs of the Shahed and Gerbera types and drones of other types in the north, south, east, and center of the country
At the same time, impacts by Russian air attack weapons were recorded at 41 locations. At another 12 locations, the fall of downed targets and their fragments was recorded.
We remind you
In Darnytsia, a railway enterprise foreman was killed following a Russian ballistic strike. The station building was damaged at Rozdilna railway station in the Odesa region.

articles.title: Russia Strikes Boryspil and Zaporizhzhia, Killing 5 People
articles.body:
A Russian ballistic missile strike in the Boryspil district of the Kyiv region on the afternoon of Saturday, Aug. 22, killed two people and injured five others, local authorities reported.
Kyiv Regional State Administration Head Tymur Tkachenko stated that the full extent of the injuries and the condition of the victims are still being clarified, though all are receiving necessary medical assistance.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to Tkachenko, the strike damaged a warehouse, a car parking lot, multiple vehicles, a private household, and a gas station.
Emergency services and specialists are currently working at the scene to manage the aftermath of the attack.
In a separate attack on Saturday, Russian forces launched seven strikes on the Zaporizhzhia district, resulting in multiple casualties.
Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration Head Ivan Fedorov reported that the strikes killed three people and injured 15 others, including a child. The attacks also caused damage to several private houses in the area.
Overnight barrage targets Odesa and Kyiv
The afternoon strike on Boryspil follows a major barrage targeting the Kyiv and Odesa regions.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russian forces launched 217 drones and multiple ballistic and aviation missiles starting late Friday evening.
Ukrainian air defenses intercepted 182 drones, three aviation missiles, and six loitering munitions, while direct hits were recorded at 41 locations.
The barrage coincided with a separate ballistic missile strike on a railway enterprise in Kyiv’s Darnytsia district early Saturday morning. That strike killed a foreman for the state rail operator Ukrzaliznytsia and ignited a warehouse fire.
Drones Attack Yeysk Seaport in Russia’s Krasnodar Region
In the Odesa region, overnight strikes injured one person and caused significant damage to transport, industrial, energy, and residential infrastructure. The Rozdilna railway station sustained extensive damage, alongside a five-story residential building, an industrial enterprise, and a sports facility.
The strikes on the Odesa region resulted in power and water supply interruptions across several settlements, prompting emergency repair operations.
Despite the fatalities and damage to the railway infrastructure in both the Kyiv and Odesa regions, Ukrzaliznytsia confirmed that overall railway operations and train schedules remained unaffected.

articles.title: Zelensky Meets Kellogg, Offers to Buy Patriot Missiles
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky met with retired US Lieutenant General and former presidential envoy Keith Kellogg in Kyiv on Thursday, Aug. 22, proposing that Ukraine purchase additional Patriot interceptor missiles to defend against Russian strikes this winter.
Zelensky announced the meeting on Telegram, noting that Kellogg traveled from Odesa to Kyiv to participate in a Veterans Forum. The president thanked Kellogg for demonstrating respect for Ukrainian soldiers defending the Euro-Atlantic region.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The discussions focused on the intensifying Russian attacks on civilian and infrastructure targets. Zelensky emphasized that anti-ballistic defense remains the top priority.
He briefed Kellogg on Ukraine’s ongoing work with European partners to establish a comprehensive anti-ballistic shield, stressing that a steady supply of Patriot interceptors is indispensable for the upcoming winter.
“Ukraine is ready to buy them, and any efforts in this direction are important,” Zelensky stated.
Proposals for a new defense alignment
Kellogg’s late-summer visit was anticipated since May, with expectations that his trip would focus on security guarantees, frontline dynamics, and potential frameworks for a negotiated end to the war.
In statements made earlier this year, Kellogg urged Moscow to negotiate, arguing that Russia was failing to achieve its strategic objectives. However, he also suggested that Ukraine should be cautious in its requests for additional aid, asserting that the defense of Ukraine is primarily a “European issue” that European allies should lead.
Ukraine Sanctions Five Russian Rusal Aluminum Enterprises
Kellogg has also been highly critical of NATO, previously describing the alliance as “cowardly” regarding its stance on Iran. He has proposed creating an alternative defense bloc comprising nations willing to take a more active military role.
He identified Ukraine as an effective partner for this proposed alignment – alongside Australia, Germany, Japan, and Poland – stating that Kyiv has “proven to be a good ally.”

articles.title: Intelligence: Putin ordered secret biolab built on island, so protected that fishing is banned, and its own guards fear infection
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defense Intelligence (HUR) says it has found evidence that Russia is running a network of secret biolabs. It was discovered on Lisy Island in Russia's Tver Oblast, where Russia conducts experiments with dangerous viruses and pathogens for military purposes.
Since Russia started its war against Ukraine, Moscow has repeatedly claimed Ukraine hosts secret US-funded biological weapons labs, a narrative it used to help justify its invasion, and which international bodies have rejected. The UN said in 2022 it was not aware of any biological weapons program in Ukraine, and Ukraine, which denies ever developing such weapons, now points the same charge back at Russia.
What HUR alleges
The facility has an official name and origin. The object in the middle of the Vyshnevolotsk reservoir, called the "Center for Experimental Physiology", was created on the orders of Russian President Vladimir Putin to "ensure the defense capability and security" of the country, according to HUR.
Since 2023, the waters around the island housing biological laboratories have been closed to fishing, swimming and boating, having been designated a “specially protected area of regional significance.”
The facility is protected from the air by air-defense missile crews, while the Kremlin has placed Defense Minister Andrei Belousov in charge of its security. Soldiers guarding the site have privately expressed fears of being infected with an unknown “nasty bug.”
HUR warns of a contamination risk
HUR has framed the lab's location as a hazard. The reservoir supplies fresh water to several settlements, including the town of Vyshnii Volochok, and feeds the Tvertsa River, which flows into the Volga River.
If dangerous pathogens or chemicals from the labs entered the reservoir, the consequences of epidemics and infections could be catastrophic not only for the region's population but for all of Russia.
HUR links it to a 2026 epidemic
The report has connected the lab to a recent outbreak. In spring 2026, an epidemic of foot-and-mouth disease in cattle broke out in Russia, which the Kremlin tried to hide from the world and its own population, HUR said.
It is not excluded that this and other similar cases could be the result of failed Russian experiments with viruses, bacteria, and other pathogens, HUR suggested. That claim, like the existence and purpose of the lab itself, rests on HUR's account and cannot be independently verified, but the accusation lands against the documented history of Russia weaponizing the biolab narrative against others.

articles.title: Russian forces strike Ukrainian military airfield, energy facilities over past day
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 22. /TASS/. Russian troops delivered attacks on a military airfield as well as fuel, energy and transport infrastructure, supplying the Ukrainian army, over the past 24 hours, Russia's Defense Ministry reported.
"Operational/tactical aircraft, attack unmanned aerial vehicles, missile troops and artillery of the Russian battlegroups struck a military airfield, fuel and energy and transport infrastructure facilities, used by the Ukrainian army, storage sites for unmanned aerial vehicles and their components, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries in 146 locations," the ministry specified.
Russian air defenses downed 11 glide bombs and 1,053 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over the past day, Russia’s top brass said in a daily report on Saturday. "Air defenses downed 11 glide bomb and 1,053 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the report reads.
The Ukrainian army lost some 1,370 troops as a result of actions by Russian battlegroups in the zone of the special military operation during the past day, Russia’s top brass reported on Saturday.
According to Russia’s top brass, the enemy lost more than 200 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup North, over 220 personnel from actions by the Battlegroup West, and more than 250 troops from actions by the Battlegroup South. The Battlegroup Center inflicted over 360 casualties on Ukrainian troops, more 310 enemy troops were lost in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup East, and roughly 30 Ukrainian servicemen were lost from actions by the Battlegroup Dnepr.

articles.title: France to give new interceptor missiles to Ukraine, Macron says
articles.body:
"It is crucial to provide Ukraine with all the necessary means to defend its airspace and thwart this aggression," Macron wrote in a post on X.
French President Emmanuel Macron announced on Saturday that France would deliver new interceptor missiles to Kyiv following a major Russian attack on a shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih in central Ukraine.
Ukrainian authorities said Russia launched two waves of drone attacks on the city on Friday, killing at least 16 people and injuring 130 others, including 23 children.
The attack on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown has prompted condemnation from leading figures across Europe, with Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, calling it "terror by design."
In a post on X, Macron said he had spoken with Zelenskyy following the daylight "double strike" on Kryvyi Rih and that he had expressed his "horror" and "deep concern" over the incident.
"It is crucial to provide Ukraine with all the necessary means to defend its airspace and thwart this aggression," he wrote, adding that he had informed Zelenskyy of Paris' "increased support, including the deployment of interceptors."
"We must also continue to increase the pressure on Russia as long as it chooses to refuse to halt the fighting and make peace," he added.
Zelenskyy said in a separate post that the pair had spoken for close to two hours, touching on Ukraine's air defence needs, funding, and communications with Washington, among other things.
"We agreed to accelerate the delivery of the latest French equipment and missiles. Thank you for confirming your readiness to provide licenses for the production of missiles," Zelenskyy wrote.
Kyiv has long been pleading with allies for more interceptor missiles as it continues to fend off Russian missile and drone attacks.
Ukraine strikes back
Ukraine launched its own strikes against Russia over the last 24 hours, hitting the Novokuybyshevsk oil refinery, a logistics hub in the Samara region, and targets in the Black Sea, per Zelenskyy.
Kyiv has been ramping up its so-called "long-range sanctions" on Russia in recent months as it seeks to hamper the Russian economy and grind down Vladimir Putin's war machine.
It has particularly targeted energy infrastructure sites such as oil refineries, depots, and terminals as part of this strategy.

articles.title: Germany Pledges €60M, Advances Patriot Talks in Kyiv
articles.body:
Germany will provide an additional €60 million ($70.1 million) in aid to Ukraine, while negotiations with international partners to secure additional Patriot interceptor missiles are progressing, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul announced in Kyiv on Saturday, Aug. 22.
During a joint press conference with Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha, Wadephul stated that discussions with European and other allies regarding the provision of further air defense capabilities have been positive, RBС-Ukraine and Interfax-Ukraine reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He indicated that he expects a favorable outcome and plans to continue the discussions next week, including a meeting with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Wadephul emphasized the urgency of supplying additional air defense systems, stating that the outcome of the war must ensure the rule of law prevails over the “law of the jungle.”
The newly announced financial assistance includes €50 million ($58.4 million) in humanitarian aid and a €10 million ($11.7 million) contribution to the NATO Comprehensive Assistance Package (CAP) for Ukraine.
The €50 million in humanitarian assistance will be directed to UN organizations and NGOs supporting residents in Kyiv and frontline areas. The funds will prioritize the delivery of generators, as the minister noted that Russia continues to target energy infrastructure ahead of the winter season.
Russia Strikes Boryspil and Zaporizhzhia, Killing 5 People
The €10 million contribution to the NATO CAP fund will support decentralized energy supplies for the Ukrainian military, provide medical equipment for military hospitals, and finance anti-drone systems.
Call for winter preparations
Wadephul’s funding and air defense announcements followed his arrival in the Ukrainian capital on Saturday morning.
Speaking to journalists, the minister contrasted the summer vacation season in Germany with the situation in Ukraine, where he stated the civilian population continues to face daily Russian attacks.
Wadephul asserted that Germany has become Ukraine’s most important ally regarding the volume of bilateral military, political, and economic assistance.
Wadephul emphasized the urgent need to prepare Ukrainian infrastructure for the colder months. He noted that he and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot have sent a joint written appeal to multiple countries requesting assistance to ensure Ukraine can maintain its energy grid during the winter.
He also stressed the importance of a united European stance, stating that Europe must demonstrate that Russian President Vladimir Putin will not achieve his military objectives.
Wadephul added that while Germany is ready to support Ukraine in potential future negotiations with Russia, continued support for Kyiv is a prerequisite for those negotiations to take place.
Independence Day gatherings
Wadephul’s visit comes ahead of broader international diplomatic events in Kyiv. Around 10 foreign leaders are expected in the capital on Monday, Aug. 24, as the country marks its 35th Independence Day.
The Coalition of the Willing, a group coordinating support for Ukraine, is scheduled to hold a hybrid meeting on Monday. The talks will be co-chaired by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, and French President Emmanuel Macron, who will participate via video link.
European Council President António Costa is also expected to attend, following the recent opening of EU accession negotiations with Ukraine.
On Friday, Sybiha stated that Kyiv anticipates the announcement of several new bilateral aid packages during the Independence Day events.

articles.title: France to ramp up Ukraine support, says Macron
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — French President Emmanuel Macron said on Saturday that Paris will strengthen its support for Ukraine after Russia’s deadly attacks on a shopping mall in Kryvyi Rih on Friday.
Macron wrote on X that he called Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday following the strikes, which killed 16 and left 130 injured. “I informed President Zelensky that we are stepping up our support with the delivery of interceptors and are continuing our cooperation,” he said.
Confirming the phone call during which the pair discussed “first and foremost, the need for air defense,” Zelenskyy also shared on social media that the two leaders had “agreed to accelerate the delivery of the latest French equipment and missiles.”
Advertisement
“Thank you for confirming your readiness to provide licenses for the production of missiles,” wrote the Ukrainian leader.
Regarding relations with Washington, Zelenskyy said he and Macron “also discussed the state of diplomatic work with our partners and communication with the team of the President of the United States. We agreed on steps that could open up additional diplomatic opportunities.”
Macron, along with his counterparts from Germany and the U.K., are expected to co-host a Coalition of the Willing meeting on Monday to discuss continued support for Ukraine against Russia’s aggression. The meeting will be held in Kyiv, with some leaders — including the French president — dialing in remotely. Around 10 leaders, including European Council President António Costa, are expected to attend in person, reported Le Monde.

articles.title: Ukraine Sanctions Five Russian Rusal Aluminum Enterprises
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky has enacted a National Security and Defense Council (NSDC) decision imposing sanctions on five enterprises of the Russian aluminum company Rusal and nine associated Russian citizens.
The sanctions target Russia’s largest aluminum production sites, including the Bratsk, Sayanogorsk, and Krasnoyarsk plants. According to a report by the Economic Security Council of Ukraine (ESCU) titled “Salt of the Earth,” these facilities are the primary importers of alumina into Russia.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Between April 2024 and March 2025, these three plants imported over $2.5 billion worth of raw materials for aluminum production. In total, Rusal-affiliated structures control 93% of all Russian alumina imports.
ESCU analysts stated that the aluminum produced by these facilities is supplied directly to companies operating within the Russian military-industrial complex. The material and its alloys are critical for manufacturing military aviation, missiles, armored vehicles, cable systems, and components for rocket fuel and explosives.
Olena Yurchenko, ESCU director of analytics and investigations, stated that the Russian defense sector relies heavily on raw material supply chains rather than just final assembly plants.
“Therefore, strategic minerals should become a separate direction of sanctions policy: restrictions must cover importers, processing enterprises, traders, logistics companies, and other key links,” Yurchenko said, adding that this approach allows for targeting the entire military-industrial complex.
Shopping Mall Tragedy: Two Children Among Nine Missing After Kryvyi Rih Mall Strike Kills 16
Recent sanctions on stolen grain exports
The newly announced measures follow an Aug. 14 decree in which Zelensky enacted sanctions against 13 cargo vessels, 11 Russian nationals, and 28 companies involved in the illegal export of looted Ukrainian grain from occupied territories. Eight of the sanctioned ships were sailing under the Russian flag.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the presidential commissioner for sanctions policy, stated that Ukraine intends to share information with international partners to synchronize the restrictions across jurisdictions and prevent the grain from entering foreign markets.
Zelensky framed the grain sanctions as part of a broader strategy to limit Russia’s capacity to sustain its war effort, which includes ongoing strikes on military logistics and oil refineries in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov regions.
The president had previously noted that Kyiv was preparing new sanctions against Russia’s military industry and financial intermediaries. The move aligns with the EU’s 21st sanctions package adopted on July 23, which included 218 listings targeting individuals and entities involved in the war effort.

articles.title: Drones Strike Novokuibyshevsk Refinery and Ozon Hub in Samara Region
articles.body:
Drone strikes targeted Russia’s Samara region early Saturday morning, Aug. 22, resulting in a fire at the Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery and reportedly hitting a major logistics hub for the e-commerce company Ozon.
The Novokuibyshevsk refinery, part of the Rosneft structure, has a design capacity of approximately 8.8 million tons of oil per year. The facility has been targeted by drones previously, leading to temporary suspensions of operations.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
As of the time of reporting, Samara Region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev had not officially confirmed the strike on the enterprise or detailed the extent of the damage.
Later, The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported that units of the Ukrainian Defense Forces struck facilities at the Novokuybyshevsk oil refinery in the Samara region, resulting in a fire on the refinery’s grounds.The extent of the damage is currently being assessed.
According to the General Staff, the Novokuybyshevsk Oil Refinery is one of the largest oil refineries in the Russian Federation and is part of PJSC “Rosneft Oil Company.” The facility has a capacity of approximately 8.8 million metric tons of crude oil per year.
The refinery produces more than 20 types of products, including automotive and aviation fuel, diesel, and lubricant components.The facility’s products are used to meet the needs of the Russian Armed Forces.
Ukraine Sanctions Five Russian Rusal Aluminum Enterprises
Simultaneously, reports emerged on social media channels regarding an attack on an Ozon fulfillment center in Samara. The Supernova+ Telegram channel published video footage purportedly showing the moment of impact, while the Exilenova+ channel later reported that a fire continued to burn at the facility.
Details regarding the scale of destruction, casualties, or official responses are currently unavailable.
Ozon’s logistics presence in the Samara region is one of the largest in the company’s federal network. The 75,000-square-meter fulfillment center in Samara has been operating since 2022, handling the receipt, storage, and dispatch of seller merchandise.
Ozon is one of Russia’s two largest marketplaces, alongside Wildberries, and ranked third in turnover among Russian retailers in 2024. Together, the two platforms control the majority of the country’s online trade, accounting for 77% of all marketplace orders and over half of all Russian internet retail sales in 2024.
By the end of 2025, Ozon managed 5 million square meters of logistics infrastructure across Russia and former Soviet countries.
Billions in losses for Wildberries
The expansion of strikes to Ozon follows a month-long, sustained campaign targeting the logistics infrastructure of its main competitor, Wildberries.
During the Aug. 17-18 attacks on the Moscow region, a Wildberries warehouse in Bogorodsky caught fire, though the company claimed it was quickly extinguished without damage to goods.
This followed a massive strike on Aug. 16 that completely destroyed the company’s 230,000-square-meter complex in Koledino (Podolsk), reportedly Wildberries’ largest hub.
Data Insight analyst Sergey Semko estimated that goods worth 78 billion rubles ($918 million) were destroyed in that single fire.
Ukraine began targeting Wildberries infrastructure on July 18. Over the subsequent month, at least 22 of the marketplace’s warehouses were hit, representing the loss of about 2.395 million square meters of warehouse space, or 43% of Wildberries’ total capacity.
As of mid-August, analysts from Data Insight and the Association of Suppliers of Goods for Trading on Electronic Platforms estimated the value of goods destroyed across all affected Wildberries warehouses to be between 445 billion and 700 billion rubles ($5.2 billion to $8.24 billion).
The Ukrainian Defense Ministry stated on Aug. 16 that recent operations had disabled seven of Wildberries’ 10 largest logistics centers. Kyiv maintains that the marketplace is a legitimate military target because dual-use items, such as first-person-view (FPV) drones, have been available for purchase on the platform, which Wildberries denies.
The extensive damage has raised concerns about a potential wave of bankruptcies among the thousands of Russian sellers who depend on the platform’s logistics network.

articles.title: Ukraine Destroys Su-24M at Saky, Hits Primorsko-Akhtarsk Airfield
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces destroyed a Russian Su-24M aircraft and four pieces of aviation equipment at the Saky airfield in Crimea, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed on Aug. 22.
In a statement on social media, Zelensky said that Ukrainian operations continue to limit Russia’s military and economic potential.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Alongside the destruction at the Saky air base, the president confirmed that Ukrainian strikes eliminated drone relay stations in Russia’s Bryansk region, which Russian forces used to guide uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) toward Ukrainian targets.
Zelensky also referenced the most recent overnight operations, noting strikes on the Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery – located approximately 1,000 kilometers from the front line – and a major logistics hub in the Samara region, as well as operations in the Black Sea.
Additionally, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine published confirmed damage assessments from an Aug. 20 strike on the Primorsko-Akhtarsk airfield in Russia’s Krasnodar region.
According to the General Staff, follow-up analysis confirmed that the strike damaged a Russian “Niobi” radar station and 18 warehouse buildings used for storing UAVs.
Concurrent strikes on Russian logistics and infrastructure
The confirmations follow a wave of drone strikes on Saturday morning, Aug. 22, targeting multiple Russian regions.
In the Krasnodar region, drones attacked the seaport of Yeysk. Independent Russian media outlets, including the Astra Telegram channel, reported visible smoke rising from the port area, while the Supernova+ channel indicated that a vessel may have caught fire following the strike.
Drones Attack Yeysk Seaport in Russia’s Krasnodar Region
In the Samara region, drones targeted the Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery, a Rosneft facility with a capacity of approximately 8.8 million tons per year, resulting in a fire.
Simultaneously, reports indicated a strike on a 75,000-square-meter fulfillment center belonging to the e-commerce company Ozon in Samara. Ozon is one of Russia’s two largest online marketplaces.
The attack on Ozon follows a sustained, month-long Ukrainian campaign targeting the logistics infrastructure of its main competitor, Wildberries.
Since mid-July, at least 22 Wildberries warehouses have been hit, representing the loss of about 43% of the company’s total storage capacity and an estimated $918 million in goods destroyed in a single strike in Koledino on Aug. 16.

articles.title: Germany pledges additional 50 million euros in humanitarian aid to Ukraine ahead of winter
articles.body:
Germany pledges additional 50 million euros in humanitarian aid to Ukraine ahead of winter
As Russia intensifies its campaign against Ukrainian civilians, Germany pledged an additional 50 million euros ($58 million) in humanitarian support to help people in front-line regions and prepare for the coming winter, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters in Kyiv on Aug. 22.
Speaking at a joint press conference with Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha ahead of Ukraine's Independence Day, Wadephul emphasized Germany’s continued support for Ukraine, particularly after July was recorded as the deadliest month for civilians in more than four years of full-scale war.
The funding will go to UN organizations and NGOs that provide urgent support for affected civilians, including mobile sanitation facilities, housing repairs, and heating equipment. Wadephul stressed that heating was particularly important ahead of the coming winter, as Russia carries out attacks on energy facilities.
"Russia continues to attack energy infrastructure and is doing everything it can to once again use winter as a weapon," he said.
"Decentralized energy supply plays an important role — including here at the Foreign Ministry, for which we will provide additional generators."
At the same time, Germany will also provide an additional 10 million euros ($11.6 million) to NATO's Comprehensive Assistance Package for decentralized energy supplies for the military, equipment for military hospitals and urgently needed air defense equipment.
Wadephul noted that air defense equipment is extremely important and reminded reporters that Berlin agreed to support NATO's Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative and the Jumpstart Agreement with $200 million each in June. The funds will be used to purchase critical weapons from the U.S. for Ukraine.
While Berlin helps Ukraine at the governmental level, Wadephul also pointed to joint ventures between German and Ukrainian defense companies, including the development of drone systems and ballistic missiles.
Over the last year, Germany has become one of the leading investors and partners in Ukraine’s growing defense tech industry.
In May, Berlin and Kyiv launched "Brave Germany," a joint initiative aimed at advancing defense technologies and supporting innovative startups. Backed by Ukraine's Brave1 defense-tech platform, the project will provide grants to Ukrainian and German companies operating in the defense sector.

articles.title: Pentagon fires publisher and editor of US military news outlet Stars and Stripes
articles.body:
The Pentagon has fired the publisher and the editor of Stars and Stripes, the US military news outlet that has clashed with the Trump administration and armed forces brass over its partly taxpayer-funded reporting.
Publisher Max Lederer and editor Erik Slavin received termination notices, CBS News reported on Friday. The cause cited was insubordination, and they have been given five days to appeal against their dismissals.
Slavin later told the Associated Press that his firing for insubordination was “for stating in a CBS interview that hypothetical censorship of news for service members would constitute a red line”.
He also said that he stood by the principle “that Stars and Stripes must remain editorially independent”.
Meanwhile, reporter Lara Korte wrote on X that she had been fired for insubordination, too, for previously telling CBS that her work for Stars and Stripes did not mean she worked for “the Pentagon … any administration … [or] any policy maker”.
“I consider it a great privilege to live alongside members of the military and share their stories,” Korte also wrote. “It’s a shame for the institution and service members, who swore to defend the Constitution and deserve the right to a free and independent press.
Leder’s, Slavin’s and Korte’s dismissals came days after the publication reported on crew conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier that have caused concern among veteran and military health experts.
Pentagon officials had reportedly discussed firing Lederer ahead of his scheduled retirement in September. He has served as publisher of the military daily for 19 years.
“It has become clear that my philosophy of leadership, and my understanding of value and mission of the Stars and Stripes, differ in fundamental ways from the direction of the leadership of the Department of Defense,” Lederer said in a letter to staff, which was posted on X.
The outlet’s reporting on the Lincoln, which is heading for port in San Diego after an extended deployment in the Middle East as part of the war in Iran that the Trump administration started in February alongside Israel, was published on 12 August, on the same day as similar reporting in the Navy Times.
Donald Trump subsequently dismissed concerns about conditions on Lincoln in part, with the president saying the crew’s deployment had been “not nearly long enough”.
The outlet’s reporting on the Lincoln is not the only issue to have placed Stars and Stripes in conflict with the Trump administration. Heralded as representing “the free thought and free expression of a free people”, it has sometimes had a contentious relationship with its primary sponsor before evidently reaching a boiling point during Trump’s second presidency.
The Trump-led Pentagon has been warring with the press that covers it, restricting access and demanding that journalists not seek confidential sources. That led to reporters turning in their access badges rather than acceding to those demands, setting the stage for an influx of rightwing media voices at the Pentagon and a legal battle.
At one point, the Trump administration’s Pentagon spokesperson, Sean Parnell, posted on X a pledge to bring Stars and Stripes “into the 21st century”.
“We will modernize its operations, refocus its content away from woke distractions that syphon morale, and adapt it to serve a new generation of service members,” Parnell also said, invoking a term used by the political right to deride progressive social initiatives.
Slavin hinted at tensions with the military brass in July when he told CBS News that the “foxhole” he would be willing to die in would be over editorial independence from the Pentagon, which provides about 65% of Stars and Stripes’ funding.
“We need to be able to provide independent news to service members,” he said to the network. “If we can’t do that, if we were turned into something other than that, if we were public relations? Yeah, that’s the foxhole.”
Korte in that CBS story also said she was “here to cover the military community”.
“I’m working for Stars and Stripes – not for the Pentagon, not for any administration, not for any policymaker,” she said.
Stars and Stripes’ Jacqueline Smith, an ombudsman, or public-facing editor, for the publication, was fired in January after writing a story critical of the Pentagon press restrictions sought by the Trump administration. Smith later sued the Pentagon, alleging that her termination was retaliatory.
The publication reaches about 1.4 million readers daily online and via an overseas print edition. It was first published during the US civil war, which began in 1861.
Stars and Stripes became a daily publication during the first world war on the orders of Gen John Pershing.
Robert Mackey contributed reporting

articles.title: Ukraine's foreign minister reveals key topics of talks with German counterpart
articles.body:
Ukraine's foreign minister reveals key topics of talks with German counterpart
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has held talks with his German counterpart Johann Wadephul on the security situation, peace efforts, increasing pressure on Russia, strengthening air defence, security and economic cooperation, European integration, preparations for winter and Russia's frozen assets.
Source: press service for Ukraine's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Sybiha briefed his German counterpart on the current situation on the battlefield and the escalation of Russian terror against Ukraine.
The two ministers paid particular attention to the situation in the Black Sea and Russian attacks on freedom of navigation.
Sybiha pointed out that there is now an opportunity to speed up progress towards peace and that diplomacy plays a key role in this. He underlined Ukraine's firm position: genuine and lasting peace is only possible with Europe's active engagement at the negotiating table.
Sybiha and Wadephul paid particular attention to special anti-ballistic sanctions, designed to limit Russia's capacity to produce ballistic missiles as much as possible. The foreign ministers discussed further steps to implement this initiative.
Sybiha said that Germany was the first country with which Ukraine began joint drone production. This cooperation is now scaling up successfully, including in the production of the Linza attack drone and the Termit ground drone.
Quote from Sybiha: "Supporting Ukraine is a direct investment in Germany's own security and prosperity. Our strategic partnership is mutually beneficial. Ukrainian technologies are already strengthening your defence and economy today."
More details: The two sides also paid significant attention to economic cooperation and future reconstruction.
The ministers also discussed in detail Ukraine's preparations for winter, protecting energy infrastructure from Russian attacks and the provision of additional equipment and resources.
A separate topic of the talks was Ukraine's accession to the European Union. Sybiha thanked Germany for its consistent support for Ukraine's European integration and stressed the importance of opening the remaining four negotiating clusters as soon as possible.
Background:
- Wadephul arrived in Kyiv on 22 August for a solidarity visit, just days before Ukraine marks the 35th anniversary of its independence on 24 August.
- The German minister arrived in the Ukrainian capital amid Russia's attack on Kyiv on the night of 21-22 August with ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.

articles.title: Ukrainian foreign minister outlines work with partners on anti-ballistic sanctions against Russia
articles.body:
Ukrainian foreign minister outlines work with partners on anti-ballistic sanctions against Russia
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has said that all ambassadors have been instructed to actively promote so-called "anti-ballistic sanctions" against Russia in response to each such attack on Ukraine, particularly on Kyiv.
Source: Sybiha's remarks to journalists on Friday 21 August, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Sybiha said Russia must face sanctions after every large-scale missile strike.
Quote: "We have an agreement, and this was our initiative: after every strike, there should be a very swift, literally immediate package of sanctions against Russia that further targets its banking system and economy and restricts its access to technology. We have called this an anti-ballistic sanctions package. It should target the entire ecosystem involved in the production of missiles in Russia, particularly ballistic missiles."
Details: The minister added that Russia has increased its missile capabilities, making it necessary to stop this.
Quote: "We have the necessary data and intelligence on this entire ecosystem, on the individuals involved and on legal entities. Yesterday, I spoke with Kaja Kallas [the EU's foreign policy chief – ed.], and all ambassadors abroad were instructed, following a meeting with President Zelenskyy, to actively promote this issue, these 'anti-ballistic sanctions'," Sybiha said.
Details: Sybiha said this involves not only European countries but also other partners, including Canada, Japan, the UK and Australia.
"We need to synchronise this approach, particularly regarding anti-ballistic sanctions, and I am confident they will come very quickly. We are also working with our partners to be as successful and precise as possible in this regard," the foreign minister added.
Sybiha also said that partners have heard Ukraine's request for Patriot interceptor missiles to help it get through the winter.
Background: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy recently said that Ukraine needs 5% of the US stock of Patriot interceptor missiles to survive the winter and 10% to destroy "all of the Russians' ballistic missiles".

articles.title: Ukrainian Air Force: 191 Russian targets downed, strikes recorded at 41 locations
articles.body:
On the night of August 22, the enemy attacked Ukraine with missiles, as well as "Banderole" loitering munitions and 217 strike UAVs; three missiles, six "Banderole," and 182 UAVs were shot down or neutralized; strikes were recorded at 41 locations, and debris from downed missiles was found at 12 locations, according to the Ukrainian Air Force.
"On the night of August 22 (beginning at 06:00 on August 21), the enemy attacked Ukraine with missiles that follow a ballistic trajectory – including Iskander-M, S-400, three Kh-31P/Kh-59 air-to-ground missiles from Kursk, Bryansk, and Belgorod regions, as well as from airspace over the Black Sea. It also used ‘Banderole’ loitering munitions and 217 Shahed-type strike UAVs (more than 50 of which were jet-powered), Gerber UAVs, and Parodiya-type decoy drones from the following directions: Kursk, Orel, Millerovo, Primorsko-Akhtarsk – Russia; the temporarily occupied territories of Donetsk; and Hvardiyske – temporarily occupied territories of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea," according to a Saturday post on the Telegram channel.
The main targets of the attack were Kyiv and Odesa regions. The air attack was repelled by the Ukrainian Air Force, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
"According to preliminary data, as of 09:00, air defense forces shot down or neutralized three Kh-31P/Kh-59 air-to-ground missiles, six ‘Banderole’ loitering munitions, as well as 182 enemy UAVs of the Shahed and Gerber types and other types of drones in the north, south, east, and center of the country. Enemy airstrikes were recorded at 41 locations, and debris from downed targets was found at 12 locations," the Air Force said.

In the near future, the FP-7 ballistic missile with a range of up to 200 km will be tested in a strike on Russian territory. This was stated by Irina Terekh, CEO and CTO of the Ukrainian developer company Fire Point, reports UNN.
Details
We have completed the on-the-ground testing (ground tests of the FP-7 — ed.) and are preparing for tests over enemy territory, and we are also working on an extended version of the FP-9 ballistic missile. I will not name the day, so that they do not hunt us down. This (testing the ballistic missile over enemy territory — ed.) will happen in the near future
She said that their developments had long been effectively helping the Armed Forces destroy the occupiers’ logistics.
In fact, we can boast that we have become so accustomed to these miracles that we no longer pay attention, although every night and every day, FP systems alone carry out from 5 to 20 different missions over enemy territory, and they have already become routine. Everyone has grown accustomed to it, but for me, the ability to repeat the same result every day is precisely an indicator of capability — it is a discipline that is much more impressive than showing one sample or ten samples and creating a wow effect
According to her, it is more important for Fire Point to prove its capability and increase it every day.
This is a rare talent and rare capability that very few companies and very few armies in the world can boast of
Additionally
Fire Point is working on two ballistic missiles. The company calls the FP-7, with a range of up to 200 km, a cheaper answer to the American ATACMS. The second, the FP-9, is designed to cover 800–850 kilometers — enough to reach Moscow. The company promises to launch the FP-9 by the end of the year.
Earlier, Irina Terekh said that the company was financing the ballistic program with its own money; the manufacturer had received not a single budget hryvnia for design work.
In addition to ballistic missiles, Fire Point produces the long-range FP-1 and FP-2 drones, as well as the FP-5 “Flamingo” cruise missile, capable of flying 3,000 kilometers. According to the company, it is these serial products that generate the money for the missile program.

Ukraine Strikes Russian Akhtubinsk Airfield, Damaging Su-34 Fighter-Bomber
